item.title: F1 2026 Las Vegas GP starting grid after five penalties
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: The starting grid for Formula 1's 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix is a very different picture from the qualifying result thanks to multiple grid penalties. Kimi Antonelli topped qualifying, but he won't start from pole position because he has a five-place grid penalty for taking the new Mercedes ADUO turbocharger this weekend. He'll start from sixth place instead.Oscar Piastri qualified seventh, but he'll start 17th because he took the new ADUO turbocharger (his penalty is twice that of Antonelli's because it's his first turbocharger breach, while Antonelli's is his second). Carlos Sainz will move back six of his 10 places from 14th to 20th while Lance Stroll will go from 20th to 21st for a 10-place grid penalty. Ollie Bearman will remain 22nd and last after his 35-place engine penalty. item.title: Plastic bag and a 'horrendous' weakness hurt Norris in Vegas
item.author: Ben Anderson
item.content:encoded: Lando Norris called McLaren's straightline speed "shocking" and "horrendous" after missing out on pole position for Formula 1's 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix.Norris was fourth fastest in Q3 and will start the race third on the grid thanks to a grid penalty for new world champion and pole winner Kimi Antonelli, but was frustrated to be 0.351 seconds off the pace."We're just shocking in the straights," Norris said. "Like, horrendous in the straight. "My lap was very good and it was easily my best lap. But to Kimi, we're eight tenths off in the last sector. "He has a perfect tow and he does a very good job. But comparing to most other people, we're too far off. "I have to start my lap 1.5 seconds off the car ahead, which means in every corner I'm losing at least a half a tenth to a tenth because of how much downforce I'm losing. "There's obviously a bigger gain at the end of the day in having a good slipstream, but we're having to make up for a pretty terrible loss of straightline speed and therefore we have to harm our cornering speed. "So we just haven't got the right balance, all in all, in terms of downforce, drag. It's made our life impossible to fight for our pole."Team principal Andrea Stella also offered an unusual extra mitigating factor on Norris's side. "I would like to mention that especially on Lando's side he has been quite unlucky, because the plastic bag got stuck in the floor and we lost quite a lot of downforce there," Stella explained. "So, considering that one tenth of a second would have made a big difference, certainly there was one tenth of a second on a plastic bag, which is a bit of a shame." Team-mate Oscar Piastri was over a second off the pace down in seventh, beaten by the Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad in Q3.And even though Norris described McLaren's deficit on the straights as something that's "been an issue all year", Piastri felt McLaren had been "caught a bit by surprise" by how much it was losing out in Vegas. "I don't think we expected it to be such a big problem," he said. "At Monza we were OK, and the strange part for us is it's mostly compared to the other Mercedes-powered cars. "So, maybe a lot of people took downforce off, and we didn't take enough off. But it seems like a pretty massive step that we were missing."Stella said McLaren had "some concerns in terms of how suitable the demand of this circuit would be for our car" because of the team's shorter gear ratios and its known weakness in generating the same straightline performance as power unit supplier Mercedes. "Certainly we have seen here trends that are similar to Monza and Baku, and in all conditions we were not particularly competitive," Stella summarised. 'Messy' or well executed? Piastri called Q3 a "messy" session for McLaren, which left "a few things that we probably will review and see if we can do a slightly better job". "Even opening the lap here, there's a bit of a difference between cars, how much energy they use to Turn 1, and if that's half a second, that can be the difference of three or four tenths down the straight later in the lap," Piastri added. "So it's difficult to get right, but I think also my laps were a little bit messy as well."As Antonelli's pole lap showed, all of this was massively overwhelmed by the towing effect - which was worth a significant chunk of extra laptime if executed correctly."I think Ferrari is the perfect example," Piastri said. "They didn't get a slipstream, or not a big enough slipstream, and they're out in Q2. "I think honestly, any of the top four teams could have done the same thing if they didn't get a tow. "So, it's a massive part of these kind of tracks in these cars, and you kind of just have to make do because maybe you can gain a tenth or two with the perfect [tyre] warm-up, but you look at Kimi, he's one second faster than me in the last sector. "No matter what you gain on the tyres, you're always going to lose it and a lot more on the tow."Stella felt McLaren had executed that part well. "What we have done better here is to mitigate this [weakness] from having really good positioning in qualifying," Stella said. "The car was pretty much where we wanted it to be in qualifying, and this definitely helped, because I have to say that it seems like with these regulations, the drag reduction when you follow one car or even multiple cars is more than in the past, and therefore there is an even higher incentive to be positioned in the right place. "I think this worked well in qualifying."

item.title: Super Formula Suzuka: Ohta takes title in dramatic fashion as Iwasa wins opener
Winners and losers from F1 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix qualifying
item.author: Jack Benyon
item.content:encoded: The rain-affected Formula 1 practice sessions meant there was added emphasis on hitting the ground running in FP3 and carrying that through into Las Vegas Grand Prix qualifying.Who nailed it when it mattered most, and who failed to deliver on their earlier promise?Here's our pick of winners and losers:Loser: Ferrari (11th and 12th)It's been a rollercoaster year for Ferrari, but a double-Q2 exit in Las Vegas has to be one of the lowest moments - even if the intricacies of this track make it a bit of an outlier.Charles Leclerc made a mistake at Turn 7 and failed to get a second lap in, while Lewis Hamilton didn't look convincing from FP3 onwards.Leclerc was quick to point out the mistake was "following a lot of frustration, building up with a lot of mistakes with the way we managed" traffic, among other things, and said Ferrari might have been a victim of a GPS issue that hit during FP3. He added that Ferrari had to be fully focused on gaining tyre temperature because that is the team's "weakness".Giving a matter-of-fact take on where he thought Ferrari was losing out, Hamilton said: "It's a big chunk on the straights. It didn't feel like we had a tonne of grip. We were struggling to get the tyres working and we were just kind of nowhere."His last lap was "very, very good", according to the team, so clearly it wasn't upset with the lap Hamilton put together.And Hamilton reckoned losing a piece of his floor in Q1 cost him "three or four tenths" in downforce alone, while he also claimed a deployment issue was a big hinderance on his final Q2 lap. Winner: Kimi Antonelli (1st)It’s difficult to resist the Vegas gambling cliches when it comes to Antonelli's Q3.He made the risky decision to back off at Turn 5 and drop to the back of the pack. Had he arrived at the line a couple of seconds later, he wouldn't even have been able to start his lap.Instead, he made it just in time and found himself in the perfect place to pick up a monster, multi-car tow to the line at the end of the lap, setting the fastest time and minimising the pain of his five-place engine grid penalty brilliantly.Albeit perhaps a touch fortunate, it was a good example of how beautifully Antonelli has played things throughout this year. Walking right up to the edge of disaster in order to crush everyone.And from sixth on the grid, who would bet against him quickly getting himself amongst Verstappen and Russell in the race? Loser: George Russell (3rd)Antonelli's grid penalty will bump Russell up to second on the starting grid, but qualifying will feel like a missed opportunity given how strong Russell was in FP3, which he topped by nine tenths.In fact, Russell actually ended up slower in Q3 than he'd been in FP3, left without the tow he pleaded for.He diplomatically said "we'll take it offline, and we can talk about it" in the post-qualifying press conference, but he was clearly frustrated to have had his request denied.Not least because it led to him being beaten to (an inherited) pole by the driver who has yet again infuriated him. Winner: Max Verstappen (2nd)Despite reporting "some weird issues" with his Red Bull, Verstappen did enough to be the fastest of the unpenalised drivers.He wasn't sure if those issues will hamper him over a race distance - as they did at Austin - but he is well poised to fight for a fourth victory in six races and continue to set himself up as Antonelli's biggest 2027 threat. Loser: Alpine (9th & 10th)Did Pierre Gasly's eye-catching second place in Q2 have him dreaming of another challenge for pole position, a la Monza?Gasly didn't say as much, but what came next was undoubtedly a disappointment. Even if it was unrealistic to expect a challenge for the top positions, replicating his Q2 lap would've put Gasly fifth in Q3, and fourth on the grid with Kimi Antonelli's penalty.Instead, the prep lap didn't go to plan and, with cold tyres into the first corner, "two, three tenths" were lost in the first sector and the lap was gone, leaving him behind both Racing Bulls drivers and ahead only of team-mate Franco Colapinto - who was lucky to escape brushing the wall without more severe consequences.It's the sort of turn of events that sums up Alpine's pursuit of Racing Bulls in the second half of the season. Winner: Arvid Lindblad (6th)Arvid Lindblad already bagged his best qualifying of the year and will benefit further from Antonelli's grid penalty to start fifth.Lindblad's put in plenty of very strong qualifying laps this year - including in the last few races, which, he says, we haven't seen due to different things impacting his results - but even he wasn't sure this would be up there with his best."It was such a mess, the tyres weren't working, so I had a lot of understeer, I made a bit of a mistake in Turn 8, so it wasn't a perfect lap," Lindblad explained when asked by The Race whether it felt like one of the more special laps of his season."But also at the same time, there's a lot that's not gone my way the recent races, that's been out of my control."Liam Lawson will start two places further back, as the Racing Bulls duo again outqualified the two Alpine drivers they're fighting for fifth in the constructors' championship. Lawson gave Lindblad a tow in Q2 which "I don't think it was entirely needed, but grateful", Lindblad summarised. Loser: Haas (17th & 22nd)Haas came into Friday hoping to get both cars into Q2 and using the heavily penalised Ollie Bearman to tow Rafael Camara to a better grid position.But its first taste of slick-tyre running meant those expectations were quickly readjusted."Unfortunately, we weren't quick enough. We showed that in FP3," said Bearman. "So, yeah, I didn't get to set a lap, I was just trying to help Rafa to come through. It would have been too difficult basically to get both cars into Q2."It was too difficult, it turns out, to get even one car into Q2 - despite Bearman doing "an amazing job", per 17th-place qualifier Camara, who said he "couldn't ask for more" from his team-mate.Throw in a weird Bearman spin at the first corner in FP3 - in his words, to do with Haas's "quali engine map and how the rear brakes basically interact with the MGU-K" - that was effectively replicated by Camara in Q1, and this added up to Haas's most difficult day, performance-wise, for some time.

Game Preview: Knicks vs Trail Blazers, November 21, 2026
item.author: Moritz Wollert
item.content:encoded: As we all know, Madison Square Garden isn’t just the most glorious gymnasium on the planet and revered in the world of sports; it’s also famous for the long list of famous musicians who have performed under its unique bicycle-wheel ceiling. Now the Portland Trail Blazers are dropping by for a quick game of hoops on Saturday night, but they might actually be the one franchise that would be adept at bringing out the microphones as well. I mean, who wouldn’t want to hear the newest rendition of all-timers like or ?!Not to disappoint anybody, but the days of Terry Porter and those shiny lycra dance outfits of the Blazers cheerleaders that would have made Cory Everson proud are long gone. Today’s Rip City Rascals (coming in at 10-5) have their own way of entertaining a crowd, though, which is more than many would have expected before the season. With the return of Damian Lillard and a highly questionable move for “Pistol Petey” Ja Morant, the Blazers looked to be about five years late to the modern NBA party but atleast early it turns out they are anything but.Portland is fun under new coach Micah NoriNew head coach Micah Nori is making one of the more funky-looking rosters in the Association work so far, and he does it with a very modern, analytical approach. The Blazers shoot and make way more threes than their opponents (outscoring them by about 12+ points from beyond the arc), defend downtown better than 25 other teams in the NBA, and make sure Tony Brothers and his brothers-in-arms in the striped shirts have a living by drawing the second most fouls in the league.Most of those foul numbers might be attributed to Deni Avdija. Only Luka from the Lakers and that feaky Greek in Miami stand at the charity stripe more frequently than the Israeli All-Star from Portland, leading to some fans questioning the ethics in his basketball bravado. But make no mistake about it, he is a serious talent, big-bodied and confident with a well-rounded game that can give every opponent problems. If he will be of any concern to the Knicks is not clear yet though; Avdija missed Portland’s last two with a foot injury and figures to be a game-time decision.But even without Avdija, Portland (road record 7-3) will present a very interesting matchup for your Knickerbockers. Damian Lillard seems to be rejuvenated after his Achilles injury, and a lot about his game feels a bit more wholesome in the jersey in which he always belonged. Behind him you have a Jrue Holiday coming off the bench, probably one of the more professional, classy guys you can find in the NBA these days. Cheekily, he also still packs quite a punch in his game, giving Nori first-class playmaking, tough D, and leadership in spades. If you think rattling these two old wily pros might get you anywhere, think again.Superior depth could be a factor for KnicksYou could have more luck with some of the younger Blazers, but many of them bring certain elite skills to the table, too. Belgian baller Toumani Camara is one of the best defenders in the entire league, long, lanky, and extremely athletic. Seemingly plodding big man Donovan Clingan is getting more mobile by the minute and still hasn’t lost his knack for gobbling up boards like a motivated Moses Malone did back in the day. Sidy Cissoko is another promising young wing, and former number two overall pick Scoot Henderson, while having a nightmarish season overall, can still break out for a big one as he did against Milwaukee the other night with 27 points.What all those Blazers have in common is that they buy into Nori’s system so far and operate with a clear-cut plan on the shiny hardwood. They extend their defense, making it hard to find anything downtown but also possible to do some damage in the midrange. On offense, they move the ball well, play five-out as much as they can (using Clingan as a high screen setter), and rely on balanced scoring night in and night out. It’s a good formula, especially without Ja Morant, who has missed all but four games with a hamstring injury so far this year. The Knicks will have to touch the paint plenty to get that Portland defense moving, and they have to attack Lillard whenever possible on that end. Their superior depth could be a factor as well.If the Blazers then throw a curveball and try to actually upend the Knicks’ three-game winning streak by dragging them into a singing competition after all? No need to worry – we still got !Who: Portland Trail Blazers (10-5) at New York Knicks (9-6)Date: Saturday, November 21, 2026Place: Madison Square Garden, New York, NYFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

item.title: What explains Ferrari’s worst F1 2026 qualifying
item.author: Jon Noble
item.content:encoded: Ferrari braced for a tough time on the long straights of Las Vegas, but neither driver making it into Q3 marked its worst qualifying showing of the Formula 1 season so far.Charles Leclerc had wrecked his chances when he was forced to abort his second Q2 run after a mistake at Turn 7. He ended up 11th fastest (he starts 10th thanks to Oscar Piastri's penalty), while right behind him Lewis Hamilton was not helped by deployment problems and some car damage that he picked up in Q1. But Ferrari’s problems ran much deeper because a combination of its lack of top speed allied to the ongoing issues its drivers have faced in firing tyres up for qualifying that consigned them to their fate.And, as Leclerc openly admitted when he spoke to the media after qualifying, the error he made in T7 was a consequence of growing annoyance at the lack of pace and ongoing communication problems with the pit wall.“I think that is following a lot of frustration, building up with a lot of mistakes with the way we managed everything, traffic and other things,” he explained. “That doesn't help, particularly on a track like this where it's all about tyres. You've got to put tyres in the right window.“I was more looking in my mirrors and trying to understand the traffic myself, that it makes it very difficult to do anything.”Ferrari's well-known power unit weakness was particularly costly in Vegas. “I'm just very disappointed,” he said. “We were expecting, and we lost one second down the straight - which is crazy. It's expected, and that makes it very, very difficult.“On a track like this, it's the most power-sensitive track of the season, so we expected to have a hard time. But I was expecting to go through Q3.”Hamilton said Ferrari wasn't blind to Las Vegas being a more challenging weekend, but he agreed the outcome was worse than anticipated.We knew long straights and stuff was going to be challenging, but the gap seems to be a little bit more than I anticipated in the straightline,” he said.“It's not insignificant. It's a big chunk on the straights. And then I don't know, just grip-wise, it didn't feel like we had a tonne of grip. We were struggling to get the tyres working and we were just kind of nowhere." Hamilton felt, however, that even in spite of the tyre and top speed problems, the potential was still within the car to make it to Q3 – taking into account the aero deficit from damage and energy management issues.We lost a piece of the floor on the first or second lap of Q1. The car balance shifted and we lost three or four tenths [points] of downforce,” he said. “After that we were struggling more so with sliding, basically from the get-go.“My lap was really good at the end, but I did the best I could with what I had. But then we lost something like six tenths just in deployment. I think without that we would have been in Q3. But otherwise, I was happy with my lap.” Another element that came under the spotlight was how the team executed qualifying, as Ferrari struggled for track position and didn't elect to play the slipstream game that many others were doing. Leclerc said that Ferrari had not gone down that route because it did not think a good tow would offer anywhere near the benefits of having tyres in the perfect operating window, considering how much it has struggled this year in managing its rubber.“I mean, that was not discussed,” he said. “We thought that tyres were just everything. Keeping just the temperature in the tyres was the most important for us.“We know it's our weakness. We've got to push. Even in the cool-down laps, we've got to push to keep the tyres high.“I don't know if the others are facing the same issues as we do, but when you have that problem, then it's very difficult to wait for two cars, and to time it well, because that requires you to go slower than what you can. It's very, very tricky for us to keep those tyres up.”There were also communication problems again with traffic management, but Leclerc wanted to understand better if GPS problems the team had suffered in practice had played a part in making things difficult in qualifying.“I don't know what was the reason for that today,” he said. “I know this morning we had a lot of problems on GPS. If that was a problem today, then it's understandable.“Otherwise, we just need to make sure that in those critical moments we get everything right. He added: “If it's a GPS issue, which doesn't necessarily come from us, then it's something that we cannot do much, and today was painful. "But if it comes from us, I do agree we need to look at it and obviously improve, because particularly in the critical moments like this, we need to be there, and we didn't.”

Russell slams Verstappen after Las Vegas GP practice clash: ‘He walks around like he’s bigger and better than everyone’
Russell won't accept being 'screwed over' by Verstappen
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: George Russell has accused Max Verstappen of “walking around like they’re bigger and better than everyone else” after they clashed in practice at Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix.Russell and Verstappen banged wheels at Turn 14 during FP3 with the stewards issuing Verstappen with a warning for moving under braking.Neither was impressed and both were clearly still frustrated with the incident after a qualifying session that ensured they’ll share the front row together in Las Vegas, with Verstappen moving up to pole thanks to Kimi Antonelli's engine penalty. With Russell second, the duo will likely face off into Turn 1 in the grand prix proper.“I think a warning was fine. There's nothing in the rules to say you cannot overtake someone who is starting a lap, but when you do this, you are screwing this person over, and he does this week in, week out with many drivers, and everybody accepts it,” Russell told Sky Italia.“I'm not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this, and walk around like they're bigger and better than everyone else.“So, yeah, somebody's got to stand up to that guy.”Russell and Verstappen have history as Russell claimed Verstappen said he was going to “put me on my f***ing head in the wall" before the 2024 Qatar Grand Prix after Verstappen lost pole position to a grid penalty for impeding Russell.Both drivers were asked about the latest incident in FP3 in a clearly frosty post-qualifying top-three press conference, with Kimi Antonelli dividing them.“Nothing happened” Verstappen simply said when asked about it, while Russell said “no confusion, it was pretty clear I think”.The FIA announced earlier in the Vegas weekend that F1 would use full-time professional stewards for the first time from 2027.Russell called that move “fantastic”, saying “Formula 1 was probably the only high-level sport that would have volunteer referees or stewards…there's a lot of stewards that are great at what they do but when there isn't the consistency everybody interprets a situation very slightly differently.“If you have the same three same four week in week out we'll all know what what they're thinking. I'm very glad to hear that's come to fruition.”

item.title: Penalised Antonelli beats Verstappen with both Ferraris out in Q2
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: Kimi Antonelli topped qualifying at Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix, but Max Verstappen will start from pole position because of the Mercedes driver’s grid penalty, and both Ferrari's failed to make the pole fight.Antonelli has a five-place grid penalty for taking the updated Mercedes ADUO turbocharger this weekend, but he minimised the damage of that beautifully in Q3.Antonelli gambled by dropping back from a squabbling pack of cars on the final runs as he ended up crossing the line with only a couple of seconds to spare.But that turned out perfectly as he was in the ideal track position to pick up a huge slipstream from multiple cars at the end of the lap to set a 1m33.893s.That was two and a half tenths quicker than Max Verstappen, who couldn’t improve on his second Q3 run.But he’ll start from pole position because of Antonelli’s penalty and will share the front row of the grid with the man he clashed with in practice, George Russell.Russell asked Mercedes for a tow from Antonelli, which didn’t transpire.Lando Norris was fourth for McLaren ahead of Isack Hadjar and Arvid Lindblad’s Racing Bulls, who was a career-best sixth.Oscar Piastri was seventh but he has to serve a 10-place grid penalty.Liam Lawson was eighth ahead of Alpine’s Pierre Gasly, who had been second in Q2. Team-mate Franco Colapinto rounded out the top 10, after brushing the wall.The biggest shock of qualifying proved to be a double Ferrari Q2 elimination, the first time the team has failed to get a car into Q3 since Imola last year.Lewis Hamilton was struggling throughout FP3 and qualifying, and looked vulnerable to an early exit from the start.But team-mate Charles Leclerc ended up joining him in the danger zone after he made an error into Turn 7, ruined his lap and then fell short of making the chequered flag for another attempt.As others improved, that meant Leclerc and Hamilton were shuffled down to 11th and 12th.Behind them were the Audis and Williams, with Nico Hulkenberg leading Carlos Sainz, Gabriel Bortoleto and Alex Albon.Rafael Camara was knocked out in 17th in his second-ever F1 qualifying session, seven hundredths away from a second successive Q2 session.Sergio Perez was 18th for Cadillac - his best qualifying since Monaco - even though he was left without a tow from his team-mate Valtteri Bottas on his lap, as in Bottas’s words, “We lost each other.”Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll were 19th and 20th for Aston Martin, ahead of Bottas and Bearman, who sacrificed his qualifying session to tow Camara, because of his huge grid penalty.1 Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes) 1m33.893s2 Max Verstappen (Red Bull) +0.258s3 George Russell (Mercedes) +0.331s4 Lando Norris (McLaren) +0.351s5 Isack Hadjar (Red Bull) +0.699s6 Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls) +0.775s7 Oscar Piastri (McLaren) +1.006s8 Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls) +1.197s9 Pierre Gasly (Alpine) +1.212s10 Franco Colapinto (Alpine) +1.421s11 Charles Leclerc (Ferrari) 1m35.197s +0.111s (gap to Q3)12 Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari) +0.167s13 Nico Hulkenberg (Audi) +0.374s14 Carlos Sainz (Williams) +0.555s15 Gabriel Bortoleto (Audi) +0.907s16 Alex Albon (Williams) +1.039s17 Rafael Camara (Haas) 1m36.220s +0.071s (gap to Q2)18 Sergio Perez (Cadillac) +1.234s19 Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin) +1.251s20 Lance Stroll (Aston Martin) +1.401s21 Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac) +1.452s22 Ollie Bearman (Haas) no time

item.title: Yankees news: Loáisiga back; Gil, Cruz cut loose
item.author: Nick Power
item.content:encoded: MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: As John covered yesterday morning, the Yankees have brought Jonathan Loáisiga back into the fold, securing another deal with a familiar face in the early days of free agency to augment their bullpen. The 32-year-old agreed to a two-year, $18 million contract with a club option for 2029.Loáisiga spent eight years in pinstripes, making 193 appearances while struggling to stay healthy. He returned to form in a major way in his sole season in Arizona last year, posting a 2.42 ERA in 67 innings. The right-hander pitches off an exceptional sinker, which sat at 97.9 mph last year and helped him to an elite 55.8 percent ground-ball rate (though he uses the sinker a little less than his peak Yankees days). Loáisiga joins the re-signed David Bednar and Tim Hill as bullpen fortifications, with fellow free agent Paul Blackburn another name linked to New York.MLB Trade Rumors | Anthony Franco: The offseason giveth, and the offseason taketh away. The Yankees parted ways with a pair of pitchers Friday, choosing to non-tender Fernando Cruz and Luis Gil. Each was projected to earn $2.3 million in arbitration. Cruz was a top late-inning option the past two seasons but suffered a partially torn UCL down the stretch last year. For the Yankees, that injury and the fact that Cruz will turn 37 in March made him expendable. For Gil, who won the AL Rookie of the Year in 2024, it was a precipitous fall from grace. Shoulder injuries and ineffectiveness limited the right-hander to 20 appearances over the past two years and, despite the fact he’s still only 28, the Yankees felt Gil no longer had a future in pinstripes.The Yankees did tender contracts to their other six arbitration-eligible players: José Caballero, Luis García Jr., Clarke Schmidt, Anthony Volpe, Ryan Weathers and Austin Wells.FanGraphs | Davy Andrews: The signings of Loáisiga and Hill continue the Yankees’ trend of prioritizing ground balls over strikeouts from their bullpen arms. Hill’s is an extreme case — the southpaw comfortably led baseball with a 68.8 ground-ball rate but got torched when opponents did put the ball in the air, allowing homers on nearly 31 percent of fly balls. Loáisiga’s arsenal was tweaked by the Diamondbacks last year; his four-seamer, previously an afterthought, became a viable third pitch against which opponents hit .148. He also regained speed on his fastballs, perhaps the most critical element in his resurgence.MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: For the 15th year, Brian Cashman participated in the Sleep Out, spending a cold November night outside in a sleeping bag to raise money for Covenant House, a non-profit that provides support for unhoused youth. He does this despite the many memes it inspires of the Yankees GM sleeping on the job, telling the , “I’ll take all those shots for a good cause.” During the event, Cashman gave some updates on the free agency process, which he equates to “drinking out of a fire hose right now,” due to the rush to make acquisitions before the looming lockout. He celebrated the re-signing of Bednar and Hill to fortify the bullpen, acknowledged he’s “having conversations” about upgrading at third, and declined to anoint Spencer Jones as the presumptive starter in center.MLB Trade Rumors | Charlie Wright: Another topic of conversation at the Sleep Out was Jasson Domínguez. Cashman noted that the Martian is “pounding the ball in winter ball,” adding that he’s been fielding calls about the 23-year-old former phenom. It remains to be seen what the Yankees GM would be looking for in an exchange for Domínguez, who has disappointed early in his MLB career but still features an enticing raw skill set. The outfielder has a 1.069 OPS with seven extra-base hits and 12 RBI in 12 Dominican Winter League games.FanGraphs | Eric Longenhagen: FanGraphs released their updated rankings of the Yankees’ top 37 prospects Friday. The upshot is that the system is below average overall and particularly threadbare among position players. The Yankees have more promising pitching talent, as eight of the team’s top 10 prospects are hurlers. Topping the list, though, is shortstop Dax Kilby. Evaluators love the 20-year-old’s swing and defensive profile; his ascent has been slowed by injury but Longenhagen suggests a “Gunnar Henderson-esque turn” is within the realm of possibility. Carlos Lagrange and Elmer Rodríguez follow as the top pitching prospects.FanGraphs | David Laurila: The number-28 prospect on the list, Antonio Gomez, made a fortuitous decision before the start of the 2026 season. A strong defensive catcher whose offensive profile had stalled out, the Yankees farmhand flipped to the other end of the battery. The early returns from the mound have been strong; the 25-year-old features a four-seamer sitting in the high 90s, a sinker, and a slider, with encouraging control for a recent convert. Gomez’s 16.1-inning audition between A-ball and the Arizona Fall League are enough to encourage some evaluators to now consider him a legitimate prospect.

item.title: Why Verstappen escaped grid drop for Russell practice clash
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: Max Verstappen escaped with a warning for his clash with George Russell in final practice at Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix.Verstappen and Russell bizarrely banged wheels while going side-by-side through Turn 14 in the dying moments of FP3 and they had to see the stewards before qualifying.Verstappen and Liam Lawson had been given a one-place grid penalty for a practice run-in in Mexico, but in Las Vegas, the stewards ultimately ruled that a warning for Verstappen was sufficient.The stewards explained that “the drivers discussed the informal gentlemen's agreements concerning the preparation for a flying lap and the conduct expected between drivers in such situations" but decided "such informal understandings were of limited relevance to the assessment of the incident".“The decisive considerations were the actual movements of both cars and their relative positions," the stewards document continued.“The stewards therefore examined the braking and change of direction of Verstappen, the evasive manoeuvre and positioning of Russell and taking into account the applicable driving standards guidelines.“The stewards considered that Verstappen’s change of direction under braking was unpredictable and contributed to the situation in which Russell had to move to the inside to avoid contact.“While the stewards did not consider the manoeuvre sufficiently serious to warrant a more severe penalty, they concluded that changing direction under braking in these circumstances fell below the standard of driving expected.“Taking into account the circumstances of the incident, the stewards determined that a driver warning was appropriate.”Ultimately, the Las Vegas incident has been judged as a simple moving-under-braking offence. The Mexico incident with Lawson resulted in grid drops because both drivers, in the words of the stewards, “behaved in a manner that was considered unacceptable”, and it came directly after a warning to all teams to avoid such practice incidents.No further action was taken over Verstappen’s other FP3 Vegas incident with Franco Colapinto’s Alpine because of “mitigating elements”, including Verstappen experiencing an engine issue earlier in the lap and Verstappen being surprised that Colapinto was overtaking him, given neither was on a push lap.Elsewhere, Alex Albon was handed a reprimand for “unpredictable and potentially dangerous” movement in front of Isack Hadjar’s Red Bull in the same session.

item.title: Russell and Verstappen make contact in final Vegas F1 practice
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: George Russell was fastest in the final practice session at Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix, despite a bizarre late-session run-in with Max Verstappen. Russell and Verstappen were fighting tooth and nail into Turn 14 in the dying moments of the session and were quickly noted by the stewards, who will investigate the incident after FP3. Verstappen passed Russell, who then tried to re-pass Verstappen, with the duo banging wheels through Turn 14. Verstappen told his Red Bull team Russell “pushed me into the barriers”. That wasn’t the only incident in FP3, as the stewards are also investigating an incident between Verstappen and Franco Colapinto’s Alpine. Russell’s session-topping 1m34.041s was comfortably the quickest time of the session and the event so far, given FP3 was the first dry session of the weekend. World champion team-mate Kimi Antonelli was second fastest but 0.911 seconds slower than Russell. He’s taking a five-place grid penalty this weekend for taking the new ADUO turbocharger. On theoretical laptimes (combined using a driver’s best three sectors), Liam Lawson was actually second fastest, 0.618s slower than Russell’s theoretical best. In reality, Lawson’s fastest time was actually only seventh quickest, 1.361s off the pace.Lando Norris’s McLaren was third quickest, 0.974s off, with Charles Leclerc’s Ferrari fourth and Colapinto’s Alpine an impressive fifth. item.title: Yankees non-tender Fernando Cruz, Luis Gil
item.author: Peter Brody
item.content:encoded: The deadline to tender contracts to arbitration-eligible players arrived at 5pm ET on November 20th, and the Yankees have decided to non-tender Fernando Cruz and Luis Gil. The pair of right-handed pitchers become free agents, while Luis García Jr., Anthony Volpe, Ryan Weathers, Clarke Schmidt, Austin Wells, José Caballero, and Heliot Ramos have the next few months to decide whether to accept the Yankees’ offer or submit their own offers as the initial step in negotiating a salary for 2027.Should both parties fail to agree on a number, the case would be submitted to an arbitration hearing. These hearings typically occur in February — subject to change due to the looming expiry of the CBA and expected owner lockout of the players — with the arbitration panel resolving the case by awarding the figure tendered by either the club or the player as opposed to a midpoint of those two figures. The decision to non-tender Cruz and Gil does not come as much of a surprise. Both players were tabbed to earn $2.3 million in 2027 according to MLB Trade Rumors’ arbitration projections — an affordable amount that the Yankees nonetheless decided was better spent elsewhere given the question marks surrounding both players’ health and effectiveness going forward. It is the second year in the row that the Yankees have used the non-tender as a way to clear roster space on the pitching side. In 2025, they non-tendered five pitchers — Mark Leiter Jr., Ian Hamilton, Scott Effross, Jake Cousins, and Michael Arias — out of their 14 arbitration-eligible players. Our own Andrés Chávez identified Gil as a non-tender candidate at the beginning of the month. It has been a precipitous fall from the stratospheric seven-start stretch that ultimately won Gil the 2024 AL Rookie of the Year Award. He has battled lat and shoulder injuries over the past two seasons, limiting him to 20 appearances (15 starts) with a 3.74 ERA, 5.44 FIP, and 58 strikeouts in 84.1 innings. An alarming loss of velocity on his fastball and worsening command has seen his strikeout rate crater from 27.3-percent between 2021-2024 to just 15.8-percent in the last two years, creating an untenable 1.9-percent strikeout-minus-walk ratio. There were question whether Gil might rediscover some effectiveness in a max-effort bullpen role, but ultimately the Yankees decided that the experiment wasn’t worth the effort. In five big league seasons with the Yankees, Gil went 21-11 in 56 appearances (51 starts), posting a 3.61 ERA, 4.54 FIP, 272 strikeouts, and 2.8 fWAR in 269.1 innings.As for Cruz, the righty reliever became something of a cult hero thanks to his devastating splitter and enthusiastic celebrations. Arriving via trade from the Reds in the 2024-25 offseason, Cruz carved out a late-inning high leverage role by posting a 32-percent strikeout rate thanks to the splitter that allowed him to sit at the very top of the league whiff rate leaderboard. However, his appearances waned across his final two months of action in 2026, and it was subsequently revealed that he had suffered a partial tear of his UCL. The injury ended his campaign despite Cruz opting not to undergo surgery in the hope of making a late-season comeback. He was recently able to begin a throwing program, and GM Brian Cashman expressed optimism about his availability in 2027, but it appears the medicals on his elbow were scary enough to not be worth the risk at that price. In two seasons with the Yankees, Cruz made 110 relief appearances, pitching to a 3.33 ERA and 3.71 FIP with 139 strikeouts and 1.2 fWAR in 102.2 innings.It is no surprise that the Yankees tendered contracts to the remaining seven arbitration-eligible players. The only other plausible candidate for non-tender was Schmidt, who is projected to earn $4.5 million in his third and final year of arbitration eligibility. The 30-year-old righty has missed significant parts of the last three seasons to injury — a lat strain in 2024, Tommy John surgery in 2025, and a biceps injury shortly after his return from Tommy John rehab in 2026. In total, he has made just 30 starts since the start of 2024, pitching just 164.2 innings after tossing a career-high 159 in 2023. However, Cashman confirmed that Schmidt is fully healthy entering this offseason, and the righty offers a much high floor and ceiling than Gil as starting rotation depth while also representing an intriguing multi-inning relief option.With Cruz and Gil’s non-tenders, the Yankees have now subtracted two more arms from their already depleted relief corps. David Bednar did choose to return on the qualifying offer while the team has also reunited with Tim Hill and Jonathan Loáisiga in recent days, but there remains a good deal of work to be done to fill out the big-leaguer bullpen. There also remains the possibility that the Yankees could reintegrate Cruz and Gil on minor-league deals in the coming days.

item.title: F1's new V8 engine agreed - five things you need to know
item.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
item.content:encoded: Formula 1 will adopt V8 engines in 2030 now key stakeholders have unanimously agreed on the key details that will underpin the new regulations. A framework has been unanimously agreed by the FIA, Formula 1, the teams and the engine manufacturers to bring in a 2.1-litre, turbocharged V8 with a reduced electric element.This switch will be made one year earlier than planned, bringing an early end to the V6 turbo-hybrid rules that only started a controversial new era this season with a switch to a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electric power. The FIA World Motor Sport Council will rubber-stamp the plan at a Shanghai meeting next month. How key final progress was reachedA meeting of the F1 Commission on Monday, November 16 led to agreement in principle over the framework. But it required some final progress to be made for the engine manufacturers themselves to accept ending the current rules cycle in 2029 and be satisfied with the switch. The manufacturers are Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull/Ford, Audi Honda and future engine supplier General Motors - which was aiming to belatedly join the current rules cycle before the end of the decade (more on that shortly). After the Commission, a meeting with the manufacturers – which are represented in the Commission but have their own key discussion group with the other stakeholders – went through key feedback to resolve what was necessary to push the proposal to the next stage. This is what facilitated Friday's announcement of unanimous agreement of the technical framework. GM will delay engine to fitA key consequence of the change of timeline is what it means for GM’s plans. Its Cadillac team, which GM is a minority owner of alongside TWG Motorsports, joined the grid this year as a Ferrari customer on the condition it becomes a full works entry. GM had been planning to debut that engine built to the current rules in 2029, which it was willing to accept even though it would be only two seasons before all-new rules came in as originally planned. To accommodate the next rules era starting earlier, though, GM will delay its manufacturer debut so it does not have to design and build a V6 for one season only.It is expected to remain a Ferrari customer for an extra year and the rules being agreed is well timed as the purpose-built GM engine facility opens in mid-December this year, which means the full might of its development push can be devoted to the new 2030 rules instead of a split project. "For a period of time, we were working on both,” TWG boss Dan Towriss said in Las Vegas. “So, they've already got a V6 base to build off of, and working towards the V8. There are a number of designs that are in motion now.”Officially, the proposed 2030 engine will be a 2.1-litre turbo V8 that carries over “some geometrical specifics”, will feature limited hybridisation” as well as sustainable fuels, and be married to a lighter chassis. This is all part of the plan to make the engines simpler, cheaper and louder – although the extent of that last point is still unclear given it will not be a normally aspirated engine. “I look at the old videos of the old engines, they give me goosebumps – it's just that high-pitch squeal that I'm missing from this era,” said Mercedes driver George Russell.McLaren’s Oscar Piastri cautioned “I don't know if they'll be exactly like the V8 engines that I grew up watching, necessarily”, but added “I think it's firstly great that we've been listened to”. The turbocharger stays partly to satisfy manufacturer demand but also to assist with fuel efficiency, avoid larger tanks and more fuel usage at the start of races. This also helps with the stated aim of making the car and engine around 80kg lighter with almost half of that coming on the engine side. More details of this will surely come from the “detailed regulatory framework” that will go to the WMSC in Shanghai next month.However, it does appear to represent a satisfactory compromise between what some manufacturers want in terms of hybridisation and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem’s initial desire for an even bigger, loud engine without a turbo. “The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide,” said Ben Sulayem. “Our vision is clear, lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition.”What’s still to be confirmedThe FIA did not specify the hybrid element, which has been known for some time to be heading towards a 100kW base electric power contribution with an extra 100kW available as effectively a push-to-pass overtaking aid. It will give the engine more than 1,000bhp at full power but crucially, compared to the current engines, not be dependent on the electric element and therefore not at the mercy of the energy limitations that have dogged the 2026 rules since their debut. Why the hybrid element has not been exactly specified is unclear – “maybe it have some KERS or stuff like that”, as Alpine boss Flavio Briatore put it – but it stands to reason that this is being delayed until more detail can be shared about how it will work. With the 2026 rules, the engine regulations were designed first, then the chassis and sporting regulations were contorted around them - leading to a fundamentally compromised product, all because the engine rules had to be set early to get all the targeted manufacturers committed. This time the core V8 engine plan should be much simpler to align with the car design and operation, but there are still elements to decide - like exactly how a push-to-pass system should be managed and whether the active aero with movable front and rear wings is worth retaining when that was primarily adopted to assist with making the current cars more efficient on the straights.Drivers are excited - with minor caveatsEvery single driver on the F1 grid has, publicly or privately, expressed their displeasure with the 2026 engines and their consequences. So, unsurprisingly, all who have been asked about the return of V8s have welcomed the plan - from the general concept to the fact that there was a good degree of consultation with the drivers themselves. Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar said he was very excited for a “full attack racing car” and went as far as adding “I don't see why that would not be the most fun cars of all time in 2030”. His team-mate, four-time world champion and vocal 2026 rules critic Max Verstappen, indicated he would have liked it to go further though. "If it's fully up to me, of course you go back to like a V10 or whatever,” he said. “That sounds even better, but I know that that's not something realistic.“So this is good, this is for sure in the right direction."Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton’s own caveat related to the detail of the as-yet undefined regulations that will define how the engines actually work – although what he hopes for most should naturally be achieved simply by stripping back the electric side so much. “It's all good and well going to V8, it depends on how they design it, regulation wise,” he said.“And going back to the good sound because that's I think been lacking since we've been in the V6 era. Bring back the smaller exhaust and get that sound back.“And as long as we don't have the engine dying halfway down the straight, then I think that will be better.”

item.title: Yankees Mailbag: The DH question
item.author: Madison Pavich
item.content:encoded: Good afternoon everyone, it’s time to dive back into the mailbag and answer some of your questions. Remember to send in your questions for our bi-weekly call by e-mail to pinstripealleyblog [at] gmail [dot] com.With Judge getting older and needing to stay healthy, do you see a scenario where he gets more at bats at DH this season, and at some point when Stanton has his annual muscle strain from an intentional walk, Judge is fully transitioned to DH and Stanton is released? If that doesn’t play out, how many more seasons do you see Judge playing RF?Not right away, at least not with how the roster as constructed stands. The Yankees have their designated hitter spot locked up between Stanton, Ben Rice, and Luis García Jr. at the moment, though the team’s future with Stanton is currently cloudy at best. For now, the team is going through with bringing Stanton to spring training and seeing what he’s got left in the tank, but even removing him from the equation still leaves the position filled up with a hitter that the team wants in the lineup more often than not. There’s also been some speculation that the Yankees could turn around and flip García after acquiring him at the deadline as part of their effort to find a quality third baseman to complete the infield, shifting Rice back to first base. Rice admittedly wasn’t that good of a defender despite working with Paul Goldschmidt though, and the team certainly won’t risk moving him back behind the plate at this point with how valuable he is to the team’s offense.Personally, I don’t think it’s worthwhile to lose García’s bat unless there’s no other avenue to upgrade third, and with the team’s incredible starting pitcher depth as well as the prospects they could part with I think there are plenty of other routes they can consider. As for Judge, while it is concerning that the last two major injuries he’s sustained have been on maximum-effort plays in the outfield (I’m still willing to consider the Dodger Stadium wall collision as more of a freak accident, but c’est la vie) he’s still a tremendous outfielder when healthy and the team would do well to maximize the value he can bring by playing him out there as long as they can. Cody Bellinger provides excellent defense in left field, but we saw how much of a struggle the other two positions were for the team on a regular basis last year, and they may not be able to find a true center fielder this offseason to improve the defense with most options for the outfield being bat-first players. I don’t know if Judge can still be Judge out there if he’s giving 80-90 percent effort out there, but his cannon arm shouldn’t be too affected by telling him to avoid a full-out dive for the ball and that change alone could be enough.Forget rumors of Seager, Bohm, Skubal, Jeffers, etc. Boone has one year left and to spend money on long term contracts to get the same old results — start the year on fire, sleep through the summer, make the playoffs, and get bounced early — makes no sense. Why hamstring a new manager with contracts that jam the roster, let the current roster with the addition of kids or one year cheap players get through 2027, and then go crazy for 2028.We’re making a lot of assumptions here, so let’s break this down. Aaron Boone is on a lame-duck contract, yes, but there’s no guarantee that means they’ll move on from him at the end of next year — or replace him with someone fundamentally different. If the team can’t accomplish more than another ALDS flameout three years in a row, I do think it’s unlikely that Boone gets handed another contract, but why set yourself up for failure just to move on from Boone when he’s at worst a minor part of the problem? The organization should be in win-now mode with their superstars getting up in age, and while they shouldn’t take on a bloated contract for a player that’ll only have one or two more positive years at best they should certainly be aiming to put together a World Series-caliber team instead of trusting that the kids can fill the gaps. They developed Rice and Cam Schlittler from unheralded prospect status into stardom, sure, but they made it to the majors by making the team unable to ignore them much like George Lombard Jr did this season.Dax Kilby is a rising star in the organization but he’s still years away from the majors, and after him the rest of their top 10 prospects are all pitchers. The best-case usage of the kids in this scenario is finding smart trades to fill out the lineup, as they simply can’t all play. The only argument I’ll make in favor of not adding too much to the payroll for 2027 is that the team likely won’t be in the Tarik Skubal sweepstakes anyway and the other big ticket names don’t impress me as much, but if they were I wouldn’t hate it. Hand him a bag and the Yankees would instantly have the best rotation in baseball bar none, and still have depth to trade away to improve around the margins.

item.title: Martin admits 2021 crash memories still slow him at Portimao
item.author: Eden Hannigan
item.content:encoded: Jorge Martin has admitted that he is still losing lap time at Portimao’s Turn 7, the site of his life-threatening MotoGP crash in 2021.This weekend is Martin’s first Portuguese Grand Prix since his 2024 victory, after missing last year’s edition due to injury. In his rookie campaign in 2021, Martin crashed heavily at Turn 7 in a free practice session, which had left him uncertain whether he would be able to return to racing. The then-Pramac rider was hospitalised with multiple fractures from the incident, but eventually returned to racing later that same season.Since the incident, Martin has raced at Portimao three times with mixed success: recording two further DNFs before his 2024 victory. However, the now-Aprilia rider has conceded that he still struggles at the corner and is still yet to regain full confidence while riding.“For sure this track is not easy for me because I crashed quite hard in the past,” Martin admitted after ending Friday practice in 10th. “Even if I won last time, I'm not feeling super confident. I see the risk everywhere but I'm trying to get that confidence.“It's just every corner, every lap I go on that corner I feel it and I know. So I am a bit more careful than the rest but I'm just losing maybe half a tenth there.”Martin was reluctant to say that the time lost from the corner was what could have cost him an automatic Q2 spot in practice - where he finished 10th - suggesting the loss of time was “more on the last sector.”The Aprilia rider did concede though that he is more vulnerable in that specific part of the track compared to his rivals. “When you have a crash like this, like I don't know, [Turn] 12 from Qatar, [Turn] 7 here. I always, every time I go through that corner I remember.“So this is part of my life. For sure it's nice that I can, you know, I'm safe now and I can do that corner fast, but for sure I am not the strongest in that section.”When asked what it would take to overcome his fear of the corner, Martin revealed it was mostly down to “accepting that you can crash again.” “At least I try to be ready a bit more,” he explained. “Trying to get more strong in the bike at that point in case I lose the front or whatever, I can recover that crash. “But for sure it's not easy to go to that corner and think again about everything. It's not easy. Everything is so fast. For sure it's just maybe one or two seconds. But for sure till I go through that place, it's not easy."

item.title: Marquez's plan to ensure he wins MotoGP 2026 title early
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: MotoGP 2026 title favourite Marc Marquez is prioritising a minimal-risk approach to the Portuguese Grand Prix at Portimao, where he has the chance to become an eight-time premier-class champion.Marquez needs to score 14 points over the rest of the season to ensure he is crowned champion.Though he can only pick up 12 on Saturday, with a win in the sprint, this would guarantee the title as it would also deny crucial points to main title rival Jorge Martin. But Marquez made it clear on Friday this is not his priority. And when asked whether other Ducati riders being competitive - and thus potentially siphoning points off his remaining championship rivals - was a boon to him, he insisted this was irrelevant."I mean, I need to score one point to 'game over' [Marco] Bezzecchi, and I need to score 14 to 'game over' Martin," he said matter-of-factly."So, this is my main target. Tomorrow, to try to score one point in the sprint. And then Sunday, to try to score 14 points."What Marquez needs (independent of others) in the sprint, GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GPor better in the GP if the sprint is aSince his return to MotoGP action at Mugello, after mid-season surgery, Marquez failed to put up 14 points in only two full-schedule rounds - Assen and Silverstone (excluding the Phillip Island weekend given the cancellation of the main race).Marquez was only sixth-fastest on Friday, describing it as a day "that you can lose a lot and you can gain nothing" - but also admitting that he was particularly aware of Portimao's propensity for causing mistakes (which are then often punished with severe crashes). "It's true that I would like to ride in a different way, but I'm human, and I was stiffer than in previous races because I'm looking at the dangerous points too deeply, everywhere - but it's normal."I remember last year [the title-clinching weekend] in Motegi - I had a lot of races to go [to get it done], but even like this, during the weekend, I was not riding in the best way possible, because when you have that kind of advantage, you feel that you can only lose. "I'm in a point that I can only lose, so I need to take full concentration to, how to say it in English, try to control all the risks that are in my hands."But then we'll see. As we saw last year - at Motegi I won, and then in the next race I got injured, and I was out for four races."Marquez said he "felt relief" to conclude the day of running because it's "one day less of risk" - and named the second row of the grid as his "optimistic" target for qualifying, with front-row speed not really on the cards.He said he told Ducati: "Don't be crazy with [changing] the bike because it's me. The bike is the same as Malaysia, as Qatar. It's me that I'm not flowing well, and on this bike if you are not playing well with the body, you are more stiff, then it's turning less."

item.title: 'I just have to reiterate the power that we have as riders' - Lombardia protest ringleader Ben Healy emboldened as he calls for change on rider safety
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: The five minute delay before the start of Il Lombardia at the close of the European season demonstrated the power riders have in forcing better safety in races, according to Ben Healy (EF Education-EasyPost).Rider safety has been the hottest topic in road cycling since the terrible death of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal in the summer. And when that incident was followed by a series of further near-misses during the Italian autumn Classics, something had to give.Healy was the driving force behind what he calls a 'stand' rather than a protest, the peloton delaying the start of Il Lombardia, the season’s final Monument, by five minutes. But, as powerful as the delay was, and as hard hitting and articulate as Remco Evenepoel’s (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) words were, the demonstration was an example of the power riders have."I think we just really wanted to show as riders the power that we had, and that we're not happy," he told in a café close to the bustle of the Rouleur Live show, where he was fulfilling sponsor commitments. "We didn't want to just go at the Lombardia organisers, for instance. You know that's why we chose to do a five-minute stand before the race actually started, and just delay the race, and just show that if this continues, that this is what we can do if we choose to.""I think after that happened [with Tarling] everyone expected something to change, you know, and when we went to Italy, there were what, three cars on the course in separate races over three or four days? And that was pretty clear then that nothing had changed," Healy said. "There has to be a process to make things safer. And I mean, for sure, the UCI is aware of it, but I don't know how aware they are, they’re not on the ground every single race. This is clearly something that is recurring, and it just shouldn't happen ever, having a car on the course, let's just hope the UCI will listen and work with us to make change."If Lombardia was the example of what unity within the peloton can do in bringing an issue to notice, Healy prefers not to commit to what might happen if and when such a dangerous situation occurs again, or worse, should another rider die."I just really hope it doesn't come to that, you know? I just have to reiterate the power that we have as riders and ultimately what we can do if we choose to. "Mistakes can be made, and as long as we're working towards making racing safer, I think that's the most important thing. We don't want to point blame or, like, kick and scream, it’s about being productive and working together to improve the sport for everyone." item.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Clark Griffith
item.author: Kevin Winterhalt
item.content:encoded: Though Clark Griffith is the first man to manage the New York baseball team we now call the Yankees, his time in New York is merely one chapter in a story of one of the giants of baseball’s early history. That’s no shot at Griffith’s time in New York and his importance to the franchise. It’s just he had such an amazing life and career.He was already an accomplished hurler when he came to New York and became the player-manager of the club, in its first season in The Big Apple. And long after he hung up his cleats, he remained an integral part of baseball in the first half of the 20th century. November 20, 1869 (Clear Creek, MO) October 27, 1955 (Washington, DC) 1903-07 (player/manager), 1908 (manager)Clark Griffith was already a grizzled veteran when American League President Ban Johnson named him manager of the New York Highlanders (often called the Americans in the press) prior to the 1903 season. It was the inaugural campaign for the club, which relocated from Baltimore after the Orioles folded following two seasons.The diminutive Griffith (listed at 5-foot-6) was a right-handed pitcher, and a good one, at that. Between 1894 and 1901, he won at least 20 games in a season seven times. His first season in New York was also his last one as a starting pitcher, and he tossed more than 200 innings while managing the club to a disappointing fourth-place finish.Griffith’s pitching days were not over, however. He transitioned to the bullpen and continued to pitch at a high level while trying to steer the Highlanders to a pennant. In 1904 and 1906, he came close, with the club finishing in second place each season, mere games from wining the American League.Modern Yankee fans are used to skipper Aaron Boone getting himself tossed from games, though he was shockingly well-behaved in 2026. He’s far from the first Yankee manager to get the hook, of course. Griffith, by virtue of being the first manager, gets that honor. Like his modern successor, Griffith also got himself suspended for his conduct toward umpires.On Monday, August 27th, 1906, Griffith took umbrage with a safe call at first base while playing St. Louis. As a result, the umpires ordered Griffith off the field. The Highlanders’ skipper took his sweet time about it. Unfortunately for him, AL President Johnson was in the crowd, and the next day he suspended Griffith indefinitely. Yeesh. “Savages in the Box,” this was not. Seems a little harsh. But wait — there’s more. The indefinite suspension might have something to do with Griffith fighting umpire Tim Hurst earlier in the season, which also got him suspended. For that round of fisticuffs, Griffith received a five-day suspension. His ban in August lasted a week.The Highlanders bottomed out on Griffith’s watch in 1908, and in June he decided it was time for him to move on. Owner Frank J. Farrell tried to dissuade the disheartened Griffith, but to no avail.“It was fighting against fate,” Griffith told , “And I knew when I had enough. I do not know who my successor will be, but I understand [Kid] Elberfeld is mentioned for the place. If that is so, I wish him the best of luck, and I hope my successor will pull the team out of the rut and place them where they belong.”Griffith’s warm feelings for the club definitely did not last forever. At his death, the noted, “Mr. Griffith had two pet dislikes in his lifetime. One was John McGraw and the other was the New York Yankees.”Griffith’s time in baseball was by no means done when he left New York. Most famously, he eventually found himself in Washington, where he leveraged his assets to obtain a 10 percent stake in the notoriously bad Senators. “First in war; first in peace, and last in the American League,” the old saying went.Griffith won five pennants in nine years before again relying on his assets to buy a majority share in the franchise. By 1920, he’d transitioned out of the dugout and into the owner’s box, ending a 20-year managerial career where he won 1,491 games (26th most all-time). In 1924, his Senators finally won the World Series, upsetting the New York Giants. They would win further pennants in 1925 and 1933 as well.Clark Griffith is almost certainly the most important person in the history of Washington baseball, with all due respect to Walter Johnson. He’s also the answer to an obscure yet important bit of trivia. Who was responsible for the tradition of US presidents throwing out the first pitch? It was Griffith, who in 1910 asked President William Howard Taft to toss out the first ball. Taft obliged and the rest is history.Griffith was also key to baseball’s relationship with the U.S. government and military during both world wars. In World War I, he organized an initiative to get baseball equipment for every American soldier overseas. He even got President Woodrow Wilson to chip in. During World War II, he was one of the people who helped convince President Franklin Roosevelt to keep baseball playing.He’s the only man in baseball history to have played, managed, and owned a team for at least 20 years each. Clark Griffith was elected to the Major League Baseball Hall of Fame in 1946. His Senators would eventually pass to his son, Calvin, who would move them to Minnesota in 1961 to become the Twins (and become rather infamous in his own right).Clark Griffith died on October 27, 1955, in Washington, D.C. In its obituary for the legend, noted what former president Harry S. Truman had said about Griffith in 1946 when he had thrown out a presidential first pitch, the tradition Griffith started decades earlier.“Mr. Griffith is a shining example of what this great country of ours can produce.”Happy birthday to the Yankees’ first skipper.See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

item.title: Shirin van Anrooij to make cyclo-cross debut with Canyon-SRAM alongside Zoe Backstedt next week
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: Shirin van Anrooij will make her debut with Canyon-SRAM in the upcoming UCI Cyclo-cross World Cup in Ostrava, Czechia, next week, racing alongside Zoe Bäckstedt at the start of a 13-race schedule, the team announced on Friday.She has been training in Malaga, Spain alongside her new teammate and former under-23 cyclo-cross rival Bäckstedt in preparation for the intensive campaign of 11 World Cups, the National Championships and culminating with the World Championships in Oostende, Belgium in January."I'm just really excited and looking forward to starting the season because we've been watching CX racing on TV for a couple of weeks now, and I'm really curious to see how it is amongst the girls again," Van Anrooij said in the team press release."I think Zoe and I are having a good preparation camp here in Malaga, so I can't wait to be on the start line myself, and to see where my level is at.""I'm hoping that I'll reach my best level in cyclo-cross again, and then I'll just have to discover what results this will bring me," Van Anrooij said."I think the biggest goals are, for sure, the Christmas period with a lot of races that I really like – Koksijde, Zonhoven, Gavere, and then the World Championships in Oostende. Worlds is always a big goal for everyone, but I especially look forward to that, with it being a race on the sand in Belgium."After her first year racing in the elite fields last season, with nine races from the end of December through Worlds, Bäckstedt is looking forward to a longer campaign. "I'm really excited for this cyclo-cross season. It feels like it's been two years since I properly raced CX as last year was an extremely short season for me."It's super fun having Shirin as my teammate. Already for training, it's been really beneficial for me to follow her and learn from her. I'm now excited to do our first race together."Although both riders have goals for the early part of the 2027 road season, Canyon-SRAM's performance director Dan Fleeman supports their off-road ambitions."I think cyclo-cross offers several important benefits. From a physical perspective, it develops the ability to repeatedly produce high-intensity efforts, accelerate out of corners, change pace and deal with constantly changing demands. It also requires a high level of anaerobic capacity and the ability to recover quickly between efforts."Technically, the benefits are equally important. CX develops bike handling, balance, coordination and the ability to make decisions under pressure. Riders are constantly adapting to different terrain and conditions, managing their effort and finding the quickest way through a course."Also, I think that there is a mental benefit. CX is an incredibly demanding discipline where you have to be prepared to push yourself outside your comfort zone, deal with mistakes, and keep fighting throughout a race."Their calendar has been designed to focus only on the major races, skipping the Superprestige, X2O Trofee, and HG Cross."The main consideration is quality over quantity. The World Cup offers the highest level of competition, the best opportunities to measure ourselves against the world's leading riders, and the experience of racing on some of the biggest stages in cyclo-cross."We also have to consider the overall demands of the season. Both riders have important road objectives, so we don't want to overload the programme with racing simply for the sake of racing. We would rather be selective, target the important events, and make sure that they arrive at them in good physical condition."Canyon-SRAM 2026-2027 cyclo-cross scheduleFri, Nov 27: UCI World Cup Ostrava (CZE)Sun, Nov 29: UCI World Cup Tabor (CZE)Sun, Dec 13: UCI World Cup Glasgow (GBR)Sat, Dec 19: UCI World Cup Antwerpen (BEL)Sun, Dec 20: UCI World Cup Koksijde (BEL)Sat, Dec 26: UCI World Cup Gavere (BEL)Tue, Dec 29: UCI World Cup Besançon (FRA)Sun, Jan 3: UCI World Cup Zonhoven (BEL)Sat - Sun, Jan 9-10: National Championships (GBR/ NED)Sun, Jan 17: UCI World Cup Benidorm (ESP)Sat, Jan 23: UCI World Cup Hamme (BEL)Sun, Jan 24: UCI World Cup Hoogerheide (NED)Fri - Sun, Jan 29-31: UCI World Championships Oostende (BEL)The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. Forbes releases 2026 F1 team valuations
item.author: Samarth Kanal
item.content:encoded: The report puts Ferrari highest at $9.5bn to Mercedes's $9.2bn, putting those two most valuable F1 teams on par with the top half of the NFL's teams, the three most valuable NBA teams, and Real Madrid.F1's 11 teams are therefore valued at an average of $5.2bn and, not including Cadillac - which was absent from the 2025 rankings - the average is up to $5.4bn, a gain of 53% from last year. Haas has made the largest increase in value - of 87%, from $1.5bn to $2.8bn - while McLaren's value has increased 73% to $7.6bn. Scroll down to view the full valuations table.Forbes uses estimated revenue as part of its calculations: from 2024 to 2025, estimated revenue rose 15% to $530m per team. Its report says that McLaren and Mercedes expect to surpass $1bn for the first time ever in 2026 - and only the NFL's Dallas Cowboys and football teams Real Madrid and Barcelona have reached that mark.The report highlights “multiples” as a catalyst for F1 teams' growth: in 2019, F1 teams were valued at 2.3 times their previous season's revenue and the 10 teams (excluding Cadillac) are now valued at 10.3 times last year's revenue on average.This signals a transformation of F1 teams' business models over the last seven years, implying that the value of an F1 team is tied to their huge potential for growth rather than physical assets and historic cashflow. Owning a stake of an F1 team is therefore likened to owning that of a valuable US sports franchise, with F1 teams' revenue multiples now closing in on the NFL and NBA - and well ahead of the NHL, MLB, and European football.The upswing in multiples is, according to Forbes, a consequence of the 2021 cost cap (at $215m for 2026) that limited spending. The cost cap, plus Concorde Agreements, have led Ferrari, Red Bull, Racing Bulls, Mercedes, Haas, and Alpine to be profitable in 2025 - with McLaren expected to hit a profit of $200m in 2026. Mercedes is estimated to have the highest profit of $225m.With just 11 teams on the grid, it's rare to be able to own a piece of an F1 team. Sportico reported in November that Mark Walter's stake in Cadillac is being offered for at least $3bn.Liberty Media CEO Derek Chang recently said that F1 has made “huge inroads” into the United States, a continued area of its focus, while China and India “represent opportunities” both for F1 and MotoGP.In 2027, the values of Mercedes and Ferrari are projected to hit $10bn.F1 teams are 'overwhelmed by interest'Being on the ground here in Las Vegas, it's no surprise to me that Forbes is reporting a 47% increase in the average value of a Formula 1 team.I've been talking to Liberty Media CEO Derek Chang for an upcoming interview in The Race Business this week and listening to him you get a sense of how buoyant the people running the championship feel about its prospects in America. Walk through the city and you can understand why.I've been to all three US grands prix this year. There was a real commercial buzz in Miami and Austin, but here in Vegas it feels like it's reaching fever pitch. As most things do in Vegas. The team commercial directors I've spoken to are almost overwhelmed by the interest. They're scrabbling around for paddock passes or trying to squeeze one more prospect into the Paddock Club. Everywhere you go there's a brand event. American companies are practically throwing money at Formula 1.Look at what F1 itself announced in three days. Standard Chartered upgraded its partnership. Nike signed up. So did Whoop. Who would have imagined, even a few years ago, that there'd be a wearables category on F1's sponsorship list? The series is in rude health.At our Monaco event in June, Aston Martin's Jefferson Slack asked “We're valued at six or seven times revenue. Why is an NBA team valued at 12 times revenue?” Forbes now puts the 10 established F1 teams at an average of 10.3 times revenue. On that measure, much of the gap Jeff saw has already closed.How much weight should we put on the individual numbers? Forbes and Sportico published eight days apart and disagreed by $1.3bn on Ferrari alone. Over the off season we'll revisit our work on team ownership and valuations and look at how the assumptions behind both reports stack up against the deals people have actually done.Perhaps the scrabble for passes is a decent KPI for the scrabble for ownership. There are only 11 teams and yet you can usually find one more pass. If either of the rumoured Alpine or Cadillac stake sales gets over the line before Christmas, we might get a firm data point of what it now costs to get in permanently.Forbes' 2026 F1 team valuations
