item.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘The cardiac Knicks find a way’
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: The same we thought we’d never see GTA VI hit the proverbial shelves…Here’s a bunch of quotes and comments coming off another Knicks dub in Toronto. On Darko Rajaković’s coaching and the Raptors’ defensive intensity:“Darko does a heckuva job… those guys play hard, really good defensively, give us fits.”On Jalen Brunson’s late four-point play creating the separation needed to beat Toronto:“That created the separation that we needed to be able to put them away. So just a big shot. It was one of those things where the play broke down, and we kept looking for an opportunity while spacing the floor. And Jalen found one and let it fly.”On the Knicks’ late-game execution and contributions from Towns, Anunoby, Bridges and Shamet:“I thought our execution, especially down the stretch, the last few minutes of the game, was at a pretty high level, on both ends of the floor, but particularly offensively. Our pacing, our spacing, our screening — we took care of the basketball down the stretch.“We got a lot of different guys that produced in a lot of different ways tonight. Obviously, KAT continues to be a double-double machine. OG [Anunoby] was our defensive player of the game. … Mikal was good for us, especially down the stretch. And Landry Shamet was huge.”On his improved relationship with Karl-Anthony Towns and the importance of adapting his coaching philosophy:“It’s just part of being around each other. You hope your relationship with everybody grows. That’s not gonna always happen but you hope it does. KAT’s got a really good feel of how to play the game. Obviously he’s a perennial All-Star. So those things you’ve always got to take into account when it comes to trying to listen or try to adapt more to what their style of play is.“As a head coach — come in, it’s your first year, and you have an idea what you want to do. Sometimes it doesn’t fit. Offensively, or defensively. And that’s when you’ve got to pivot. And so we kept pivoting and pivoting and building until we found a nice little groove. We feel pretty good about each other right now.”On recovering from the ankle injury scare after his four-point play:“Adrenaline was pumping, and went back out there.”On Josh Hart and Mikal Bridges regaining confidence and contributing to the Knicks’ success:“This is a huge night for them, the way they played. They’re gaining confidence every single night. They’re going to continue to do great things for us and they’re only going to get better.”On the Knicks rediscovering their ability to win close games:“A lot of times when we get in games like that, especially last year, the cardiac Knicks find a way.”On gaining Mike Brown’s trust and having more input in the team’s strategy:“It’s more familiarity with the system and building that trust with Mike where he can trust me with things I see and say, which started in the playoffs. So building off that this year. Having more input and him hearing me out.”On acting as a second coach and collaborating with Brown during games:“Him trusting me like a second coach. Me and him are always coaching with each other in the game, looking at game plans and plays and maybe ideologies and things I see that can help our team win, especially in close games. Working with him and coaching on the floor. It’s been great. It’s been fun.”On how his relationship with Brown has improved since the championship run:“We just grew. We’ve grown with each other. And obviously there’s trust that has to be established and both of us trust each other a lot. And the last playoff run showed it. So just building off that trust and the relationship that was built in the playoffs and having it make our team better this year.”On Jose Alvarado’s professionalism and importance to the Knicks’ locker room:“Jose is a consummate professional. He’s probably one of the best locker room guys we have, and one of the best people we have on the bench. His energy, just his presence, with a jersey on or a warmup on, it means more for this team than what the stats show.”On his recent mental struggles:“Has been kicking my ass for a couple weeks.”On stepping up his game on Tuesday after struggling through a few games:“I think it was a step in the right direction. I think I’m obviously getting into the flow, into the rhythm of things, but today was a step in the right direction. Still a lot to improve on, but you got to start stacking days at some point.”On how his contract situation can amplify the pressure of poor performances:“That’s a low-hanging fruit. Sometimes some of those things amplify because you’re in a contract year, essentially. It’s human nature.“It’s in the back of your mind, and when you start focusing on those things, negative outcomes happen.”On trying to overcome his struggles and improve his mindset:“When you’re in the middle of it, there’s not much that can really help. At the end of the day, you just have to go out there. And I think today I had a little bit of a better spirit.”On the negative thought patterns that have affected his performances:“I’m struggling to shoot the ball, but it’s one of those things where you start looking at the negatives and that’s all you see. You don’t see some of the positives. Then it’s a snowball effect. One thing happens and you’re trying to get yourself out of a hole that you’re not giving yourself the ability to get out of. It’s about playing with that joyful spirit, looking at things half full instead of half empty.”On dealing with physical and mental challenges simultaneously:“For me, this (rough patch) is a little harder because I’m trying to get the mental aspect right and the physical aspect right. It can be easier when you’re just dealing with one of those things. … I’m battling both of those things. I’m trying to give myself a little bit of grace with that.”On maintaining a positive attitude despite losing his place in the Knicks’ rotation:“I think it’s more how I was raised [by] my parents. Treat people how you want to be treated. Sometimes the situation isn’t going to be what you want. You can’t control certain things and control what you can and that’s your attitude, your energy every day. So I try to do that.“I’m human, I have days where it’s not going to be all lovey-dovey. But I always tell myself, ‘Whether I’m not playing or not, I got the best seats in the house.’ And I get to support my teammates. So I try to go with that mindset as best I can and my teammates allow me to be myself.”On the viral clip showing him comforting Mikal Bridges on the bench:“[Mikal] is fine. We are all human. The camera caught us that time, but I probably do stuff like that 100 times during a game.”On staying prepared for opportunities after falling out of the rotation:“The season is long. I’ve been on the other side. When I first got in the league [in 2021], I wasn’t even touching the court. Then eventually I got to touch the court and get some reps in and played a huge role in the rotation.“Sometimes you get out of it. The only way to get back is stay ready because an opportunity is going to come, you just don’t know when. So that’s the hardest thing is the guessing game of when that will happen. But you work, work and work and trust that it will come in the end of the day.”On how close the Raptors came to beating the Knicks in their previous meeting:“After rewatching and rewatching and rewatching film, we played against the NBA champions and, in my three-and-a-half years here as coach, that’s when we came the closest to beating them. We’re getting better. Just one free throw and the game is completely different.”

'I'd say it’s costing people’s lives' – Safer technology is here, so why hasn’t the cycling industry implemented tougher helmet testing yet?
item.author: Emma Cole
item.content:encoded: Helmet safety awareness and the danger of head injuries from cycling crashes is growing, so why haven't helmet standards changed for years, and what is being done to improve the technology that protects our brains as cyclists?A test for how helmets deal with rotational head impacts was created and published in 2024, but two years on, the committee tasked with setting a pass mark is yet to agree whether, or how, to require it, and so many helmets are missing a key standard of safety and protection.Mips (multi-directional impact protection system) technology has long been the market leader in rotational impact technology, and you'll see its yellow sticker and protective system on many helmets. Mips technology is fitted between the inner padding and outer shell of the helmet, and allows for slippage and movement that helps reduce the rotational impact transferred to the wearer's head.Whilst popular, Mips is not the be-all and end-all of helmet safety technology, and new externally-fitted solutions like RLS have come into play in recent years, but the helmet industry – and riders – are still waiting on a universal standard. We spoke to leading figures from helmet technology manufacturers, helmet brands and independent testing bodies to find out what is standing between the industry and a better safety standard, and what the future of helmet safety might look like.Why rotational impact testing matters Cycling helmets sold in Europe are certified to European Standard EN 1078, which was last updated in 2012, nearly a decade and a half ago. It tests only linear, straight-on impacts.This is noteworthy because when the head hits the ground at an angle, it twists, and the brain is stretched and sheared because of this rotation. This can damage the nerve fibres that carry signals around the brain, as well as blood vessels, resulting in concussion or more severe damage such as a TBI.This is why many believe in the importance of testing cycling helmets at angled or oblique impacts, as this is more representative of real-world bike collisions – and indeed rotational impact is often more dangerous and more severe than a straight-on knock.Innovating external solutions Despite the lack of a European Standard or wider requirements for helmets to also protect against rotational impacts, plenty of manufacturers, scientists, and innovators are working to create systems that better protect riders and get this technology into more helmets. The Release Layer System (RLS) is a newer rotational impact technology which works by having panels bonded to the outside layer of the helmet which move on polycarbonate bearings. Upon impact, these panels absorb energy and release from the helmet, reducing the amount of rotational energy transferred to the rider’s head. I was invited to see this technology firsthand at the RLS facility in London, complete with a testing drop tower they use to assess the impact helmets absorb.RLS says its technology lowers the risk of a brain injury like concussion from 64% to 9% when compared to a standard road helmet. "Because the technology is on the outside, the moment you make an impact, the technology is able to instantaneously work rather than being in those microseconds absorbed and then having to do the work on the inside," explains James Cook, CEO of RLS. "When you increase the energy, a lot of solutions don’t work very well because there's too much pressure. That's where actually a bearing solution is really good because bearings have been used for high pressure."Cook adds that the panels are designed to survive everyday knocks and will only come apart under a significant impact.RLS grew out of HEXR, a helmet brand Cook co-founded, which it now uses to test the technology. While Mips has long dominated the market with its internal slip layer system, there is a consensus that external solutions like RLS could also work well, or even better."Reducing friction on the outside is a better idea than reducing it on the inside," says Alessandro Cernicchi, R&D director at helmet manufacturer Kask. "If you want to redirect energy, a good way to do that is on the outside of the helmet because you have quite a big surface there and you can create a big movement and so on," says Max Strandwitz, CEO of Mips.Mips developed its own external concept in 2017 called Impact Shield. However, Strandwitz believes that external solutions can be too sensitive."We were a little bit reluctant to release the Impact Shield because as soon as you have solutions on the outside of the helmet, they become very sensitive. If you drop it or if you bump into something, all of a sudden, the technology is out."Despite his hesitations, Strandwitz says Mips might reconsider an external solution. For now, Mips’ market position remains formidable. He says Mips is adding its technology to almost one new helmet every working day across all categories, including snow, motorcycle and industrial helmets, with cycling making up roughly two-thirds of its business.The power of the yellow dot sticker is reflected in Fizik’s decision to enter the helmet market with Mips. "Being new into a category, we haven't got years of people telling good stories about our helmets, and we knew what a well-respected brand name could do in terms of entering a new market," says George Huxford, senior marketing manager at Fizik. The elusive mandatory testThere are two main European Committee for Standardisation (CEN) working groups related to implementing a rotational impact standard for helmets.Working Group 11 (WG11) set a rotational test method called EN 17950, with a new headform – the dummy used for testing – which was published in 2024. This headform is regarded as more representative of a human head. It took over 10 years for the group to agree on this, and even now there are some disagreements.Working Group 4 is revising EN 1078, the standard to which every cycling helmet sold in Europe is certified and may establish a pass/fail mark for helmets with regard to rotational impact. It is this revision which would mandate that all helmets be rotationally tested as per EN 17950 and the headform which should be used in testing. The working groups are made up of manufacturers, brands, ingredient technology companies, universities, test labs, governments and consumer groups, all of whom will be impacted by what is agreed, which may be having a disproportionate effect on the decisions these groups are or aren't taking."It’s really a shame that standards have not yet adopted rotation, and I think it is the elephant in the room," says Professor Mazdak Ghajari of Imperial College London, who co-authored WG11's research on the new headform."Well, I may upset some of my colleagues on the working groups, but the truth is that over 80% [of parties sitting on the committees] are manufacturers," he adds. "They are members of the committee for good reasons; we cannot set a standard that they cannot meet or which costs them a massive amount of money."But at the same time, they told me that they spent 80% of their budget and R&D on optimising products for the current standard. Now imagine if there is something new, then they have to inject new money into understanding how their product would perform so obviously there is a lot of inertia.""There is a lot of politics which I think doesn't belong in the regulatory body for safety standards," adds Strandwitz, also noting the difference between the US and European approaches. "In [the] US, it's a much hotter potato, and they are moving and will probably move a lot quicker," he says. "In Europe, you are still having some that are a bit conservative, and that think rotation is not a big problem."My experience is that it's seriously conflicted," echoes Cook, who sat on WG11. "People are not just thinking about how they protect people; they’re also thinking about how they protect the business."There's a deadline that the European Commission sets, but then there are ways in which the working groups can collectively not align to either extend the timeline or push things back, and that's effectively what's going on. It’s just the can is being kicked down the road again, and again, and again, and I’d say it’s costing people’s lives."We're seriously keen to try and push to have at least a standard that recognises rotation, but then also push to have a pass/fail criteria that means that more helmets are going to be safer on the road."However, Cernicchi at Kask views conflict within the group as expected and healthy, since all stakeholders are represented. Cernicchi believes a cautious approach is best. "It's kind of a revolution in the way we are testing helmets; we've been testing helmets for years with linear impact, and now we are proposing to introduce rotation. You want to do it very, very carefully."The headform, the dummy used in testing, is meant to reflect a human head and was a major sticking point for WG11 members to agree on. Headforms have different coefficients of friction from one another and thus produce different results. Kask still uses the EN 960 headform in its testing but says it plans to transition to EN 17950 headforms from 2027."The EN 17950 standard is still not perfect, so we still have to work on it to make it perfect, and then we can start adopting rotational methods for certifying helmets according to the product standards," says Cernicchi. He says EN 17950 headforms made by different manufacturers produced results up to about 10% different, and experts want that narrowed before rotation can go into EN 1078."We have to rewrite it to have narrower tolerances before we can introduce [the] rotational method in the 1078 and all the other product standards."Any new headform also comes at a cost to manufacturers, which could also be a factor behind the slow implementation of more accurate headforms."If Europe agrees to approve a new headform, it will mean an investment of somewhere around €20,000 to €25,000 for a lot of companies because you need to invest in a new headform," says Strandwitz."This should have been done already a long time ago. If you look at the EN 960 headform, it's 30 years old, and it's not biofidelic. It's a magnesium headform without the nose, and it looks extremely flat."Independent ratings and testing There’s another layer of complexity around helmet testing and standards, and that's who pays for the testing and research.Brands often test their own technology in-house. Kask, for example, has its own testing protocol, WG11, and now has its own in-house testing laboratory. RLS has its own drop tower and publishes side-by-side test videos, while Strandwitz says Mips runs 15,000 to 18,000 tests a year but doesn’t publish them publicly. Strandwitz doesn’t think that brands publishing their own test results is enough, and retains some scepticism about the results we do see."For me, it will be strange if you, as the market leader, say: 'Look what we have done at home!' Who would publish a test that doesn’t come out well?" he says. "If you have a technology that is good enough, you can rely on third-party testing, and that’s what we do."Professor Ghajari launched Hiper two years ago as an independent safety rating system, developed by researchers at Imperial College London and funded by The Road Safety Trust.Hiper buys each one of the helmets it tests and does not accept money from brands, which Ghajari says helps maintain independence. "It's very important because even manufacturers tell me that they can send a helmet to rating that is different to the helmet they send to the market," he says. "It is a known fact and another elephant in the room."Ghajari adds that Hiper’s ratings are meant to sit alongside the standard as they provide consumers with safety information beyond the minimum, which is important as a high price point does not equate to a safer helmet. The latest Hiper ratings looked at collapsible and normal helmets and found that a higher price does not mean greater safety. The highest-rated helmet in the gold category was the MET Vinci Mips, which costs £100, while the Van Rysel RoadR 500, which costs £29.99, was awarded silver, and a £95 collapsible Overade PLIXI came last in the bronze category. Hiper has not yet rated a helmet that uses RLS. An Imperial College study, published alongside the ratings, also highlighted the importance of rotational impact solutions, as "the presence of rotational protection technology significantly reduced both linear and rotational injury risk in helmets". Using the new EN 17950 biofidelic headform, Ghajari says Hiper’s test repeats each impact on three samples for statistical distribution, adding that he believes Hiper’s testing method is more rigorous than that used by other leading helmet testing body, the Virginia Tech Helmet Lab.Virginia Tech uses a NOCSAE headform, and each helmet rating is based on 24 oblique impact tests across six locations and two impact speeds. The laboratory tests helmets across all kinds of sports and activities, including hockey, baseball and American football, as well as construction, horse riding, and, of course, cycling."Our published research also shows that the NOCSAE headform’s vibrational response aligns more closely with published human-head measurements than other headforms," says Steve Rowson, professor at Virginia Tech and director of the Virginia Tech Helmet Lab."Hiper’s published methodology also incorporates both linear and rotational injury measures, although its calculation differs from ours. Our methods are publicly available and published in peer-reviewed journals, and manufacturers do not influence the rating methodology or the assignment of ratings."We purchase helmets for our ratings. We also sometimes test helmets before their public release so manufacturers can have a rating available when the product reaches consumers. In those cases, the manufacturer must provide written certification that the submitted helmet is identical to the product consumers will be able to purchase.He adds that sometimes they conduct random follow-up testing to ensure that a submitted sample is identical to the retail product.In Virginia Tech’s bike helmet ratings, RLS has two helmets with its technology in second and third place overall, while helmets with Mips start at fourth place. Strandwitz argues that Virginia Tech’s current testing is slightly weighted towards external solutions. "The challenge is that in a straight impact, these solutions normally perform quite well. In Virginia Tech, for instance, that impact point is weighted much higher than anything else, but you need to manage impacts in all directions."Rowson disagrees with that notion, however."Our scoring system does not include any variable for the presence, brand, supplier, or location of a particular technology," he underlines. "We evaluate the complete helmet under the same published impact conditions, and its score depends on the measured head response. Manufacturers can improve that response through materials, geometry, integrated features, or additional components."There are other questions around independence and commercial interests in the world of helmet safety, partly due to the fact that it's a small niche and funding and personnel overlap a lot.RLS states that testing was conducted independently at the iCUBE laboratory of the University of Strasbourg and the RLS laboratory in London, and results are validated externally and peer-reviewed.Whilst helmet safety technology applies to every cyclist who uses a helmet, whether that's for a short commute or a professional race, there is an added layer of urgency, concern and danger when it comes to pro riders who are racing at higher speeds and face more frequent and larger crashes.The UCI instigated a concussion protocol and has various rules about what equipment pro riders can and cannot use, but it does not mandate rotational impact testing or ingredient technology for helmets used in road racing.Cook at RLS says they’ve been talking to UCI for about two years. He points to the speeds at which pro riders compete, which he thinks should encourage the UCI to mandate a testing standard. "It sounds like UCI are thinking about it in the right way, and they know it's on their roadmap, but we also don't want to let it stall," he says. "We're here to support the UCI; we're here to support anybody in terms of trying to create a standard that actually protects people, but we also want to make sure that if it's going too slowly, we can nudge it along by sharing data and being quite open about it."Given that we already know there are lots of people dying every year, let alone having concussions, I would have thought someone at the UCI would be spearheading this." The UCI responded: "As the process and discussions are still ongoing, the UCI will not comment on this topic. We will communicate once we have more information and details."What the future could like In motorcycling, there is already a rotational impact test standard, ECE 22.06, which some believe cycling should mirror. "Get something going and then improve from there," is Strandwitz's hope for the immediate future of helmet safety technology. "In motorcycling, with ECE 22.06, they at least did it, even with the old headform."When you do that, you can filter out the worst-performing helmets on the market, the helmets that should never be there.""The motorcycling federation has also gone above and beyond what the European standard is," adds Cook. "They've said we want to see helmets that meet an even higher performance."However, Cernicchi disagrees, remarking that he’s never seen a helmet fail the motorcycle standard, which suggests the bar is set too low. So, what are we left with? Any certified helmet is clearly better than none, but with experts who set the standard still disagreeing, it looks like rotation will remain the 'elephant in the room' for a while longer.

item.title: Castelli Alpha 150 jacket review: Warm and comfortable, but not right for the deep freeze
item.author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
item.content:encoded: Castelli’s jacket range has gone on a fair old journey in recent years. The Gabba and Perfetto have been overhauled, and everything is now PFAS-free. The Alpha 150 is the Italian brand’s most wintery and most expensive outer layer, featuring an inbuilt fluffy body warmer to really seal you in and, I presume, seal a top spot in my guide to the best winter cycling jackets. I’ve been testing it out throughout last winter, and through a fortuitously timed cold snap in recent weeks that has left the air thick with freezing mists and rich fog. I do like it as a jacket, but like many recent Castelli options I’ve been testing out, the suggested temperature range is perhaps a little too cold for reality. The flip side is that the breathability is excellent, so as long as you don’t stop, it’s less of an issue. Eight colours for such an expensive jacket does feel like a recipe for the unpopular ones to go on sale eventually, but they are all at least part of a pleasing spectrum.For my part, I tested out the ‘mango mojito’ colour, which is a posh way of saying ‘yellow’. It’s the platonic ideal of yellow; primary, bright, unfussy, and I was glad of it in the gloom versus the more subdued Assos jackets I’ve also been testing alongside it.The form is tailored but not skin-tight, with enough room to layer up a little bit underneath, at least with a thicker long-sleeve jersey and a winter base layer. You get a high, fleece-lined collar and very neat cuffs that feature a tight, stretchy synthetic cuff that surrounds the wrist, and a looser yellow main fabric over the top that I’m sure does little practically but certainly improves the aesthetics. Open up the main double zip, either through the big, easy-to-pull-with-gloves-on toggle at the top or the normal zip tab at the bottom, and you’ll reveal a Polartec Alpha inbuilt gilet. The rear panel is free-floating, attached only at the sides and top so it articulates more easily and I assume compresses less. The front is two simple panels with a low-cut neckline, so that you can use the main zip to cool the neck or accommodate a neck warmer, and secured by a smaller one-way zip. I could do with this also being 2-way, for reasons of pocket access, but I imagine Castelli envisioned it being used perhaps with just a deep winter base layer underneath. The main fabric is Castelli’s exclusive ‘150g Polartec® AirCore™ electrospun air-permeable membrane’, which is alleged to be windproof while also remaining highly breathable. To this end, it is. Castelli also claims it can ‘stand up to everything except all-day driving rain’. It can’t. If it’s going to rain, wear something else; a waterproof jacket, perhaps. It is relatively lightweight in feel. My size medium tips the scales at 324g, 70g less than an equivalent Assos jacket that I’ve been testing, but spread over your whole torso you’re not really going to notice that difference. The relative softness and flexibility of that Aircore outer fabric does make it lighter compared to stiffer, hardier options. At the back, you get a reflective piping sewn under the standard three rear pockets and above a stretchy, neoprene-like waistband that is dropped far enough to cover even non-modern jerseys, though again, I suspect this is meant to just go over a base layer. This is a good jacket; I do want to get that on record first. I do think the suggested temperature range is a little ambitious, however, and I don’t think you can realistically use this comfortably in anything below about 5ºC if you plan on stopping for any time at all. The issue comes not from the added cosy insulation, but from that AirCore fabric. I had the same issues with the DoDiCi jacket, and my colleague Josh had with the previous Perfetto RoS 3; it’s just a little breathable, so you don’t keep as much heat in as you think you will and you get a little colder than you’d like. A few commutes around 6º, with a merino base layer and a merino long-sleeve jersey underneath, it started to feel a little on the cool side, and when things hovered around zero, I often found myself reaching for my Albion Ultralight Insulated Jacket to slip over the top as a breathability modifier. The wind resistance was perfectly good; I never felt like the breeze was scything through the fabric even on fast descents, so I do think it’s just a function of just how breathable the outer is. If you’re doing higher-output riding in the winter, then it does make more sense, but for those longer, steadier winter miles it’s just not quite right. That aside, when I did get the temperature right, I found it was really excellent. When you use it when it’s a little warmer - somewhere between about 7 and 12 degrees (44-54 degrees F) - on less intense rides, it keeps you just the right temperature, and the added breathability means when you get hot on climbs you don’t immediately get drenched and then freeze.If you do get a little toasty, it’s very easy to ventilate yourself back into a comfortable range. The interior Polartec Alpha gilet thing is so breathable at the front that when you unzip the main outer zip you can feel the wind cooling you immediately.I found a few centimetres at the top and bottom of the zip undone was often sufficient to keep me where I wanted if I was cooking a little, but on the whole this was never a jacket I ever overheated in, and I feel like I’d have to try really hard and layer very badly to get it wrong to the point where I’d become a sweaty mess at the side of the road. The most I ever really had to do was take a neck warmer off. The cut is also excellent. The sleeves are long enough to not expose my wrists, even as a very gangly chap, and there’s enough room that I never felt constricted even with an additional jersey between my jacket and my base layer. I don’t think you’ll have a great time if you try and wear a thicker mid layer, as you can do with some of the Assos deep winter layers I’ve tested, but a thick winter jersey is totally doable. This brings me to the pockets; the three on the actual jacket itself are great, easy to access and roomy enough to house things like a light waterproof shell or a pair of gloves with ease alongside the usual suspects.My main annoyance comes with the fact that the internal fluffy gilet zip isn’t 2-way. I almost always wear a jersey under my winter jackets, even if it’s just a thin one. It gives me three extra pockets, as much as anything else, but with this zip arrangement, you just can’t get in easily. It’s a minor gripe, but a gripe nonetheless. At $645 or £360 it’s a very expensive jacket, significantly more than the likes of the exceptional Assos Equipe R Winter Jacket, one I would argue is superior in performance across a wider range of temperatures. While I did (and still do) very much enjoy using it, given I found it better suited to longer, lower-intensity riding in warmer conditions than advertised, for many of you I suspect you can get the same level of insulation for a lot less outlay, and while you won’t have the same breathability, this won’t necessarily be such a problem for slower cold-weather riding unless you run very hot indeed. Castelli’s Alpha 150 jacket may be the warmest the brand makes, but if you’re going anywhere near actual freezing conditions, then I suggest this isn’t the jacket to reach for, as it’s just too breathable to keep you at a comfortable temperature.For longer, lower-intensity riding at high single figures, it’s dreamy, comfortable, good-looking, and well finished, but it’s a lot of money to drop on a jacket like this when cheaper options will do the same thing in many cases. Exactly what I'd want in a winter jacket. Close but with enough room for a choice few key layers.It's simply not as warm as advertised, especially once you stop riding hard. The internal vest is great, and the hip valuable pocket is much better when you're all gloved up and less dextrous. Extremely breathable (too breathable, to be honest). No chance of getting sweaty unless you get your layers very wrong. For what it offers you can get the same warmth for a lot less outlay, and the breathability won't be too much of an issue unless you're riding hell for leather up a climb.

item.title: Knicks 111, Raptors 102: “Let it be 15 straight”
item.author: Moritz Wollert
item.content:encoded: One of the more prominent flies caught in the interwebs these days was the nomination of Robert Pattinson as the new lead for the James Bond franchise. Yes, the guy who made daughters melt by the millions about two decades ago and who always looks like the vampire that made him prominent drank all the blood from his veins. Apparently he’s a really good actor, but pardon me if I’m not acting like I’m some kind of wannabe film critic just because I like movies every once in a while.For my liking, the 007 I loved ended with the retirement of Roger Moore, a second gut punch not needed after the grim realization that Sean Connery’s time in Her Majesty’s Service was over (we ignore Roger Lazenby for obvious reasons). Before watching any of the newer films, I always much rather flopped in one of the classics, because with the world spinning faster every day, there are just some things in life I’d like to stay the way they are. Like that bank account from December before all the insurance companies wish you a happy new year or that favorite dish your Grandma used to make before she discovered light whipping cream. And while we’re at it, the fact that the New York Knicks do not lose to the Toronto Raptors.Knicks work their late-game magic – againAfter watching the Knicks almost win a carbon copy of their game on Sunday in Toronto for their 15th in a row against the Dinos, it truly feels like some divine decree puts some prehistoric panic on the Raptors in the final minutes and sprinkles just enough calmness on the orange and blue to pull it out in the end. Just like Unmitigated Gall wrote in the celebratory Postgame Thread: “Sayeth the Lord: Let it be 15 straight”. But maybe it’s also just pure and legit NBA talent taking over, and prevailing over the guys who are airballing free throws or thought it was a good idea to give Jakob Poeltl north of 100 million dollars to play basketball.Even if Jalen Brunson shot it as purely as “The Man with the Golden Gun,” late everything for New York started and ended last night with Karl-Anthony Towns. Early in the season, he looks sharper than Oddjob’s razor-edged hat (shoutout to “Tosh Togo” Harold Sakata) and, on top of it, more powerful than Richard Kiel’s “Jaws”. KAT’s dominance was on full display against a team that could only put defenders on him who were either too small or too slow. Dismantling those adversaries wasn’t even the most impressive thing the 31-year-old did, as his passing at times was as beautiful as Honey Ryder, Tatiana Romanova and Miss Galore combined.To be serious for a second: It is astonishing how Karl-Anthony Towns has turned around his career after more than a decade in the league. He is by far the most consistent Knick right now, has cut down on his foul issues for the time being, and looks extremely decisive on both ends of the court. In Minnesota, he always gave the impression of lacking professionalism, and now he looks like the most serious player on a team full of guys who seemingly laughed the last time the Raptors or Nets beat the Knicks. Maybe “You only live twice” as a basketball player, but in KAT’s case that looks to be plenty enough.Karl-Anthony Towns shines for New YorkThe “License to Kill” in the end, of course, rests with his buddy about a foot shorter than him. You wouldn’t believe it watching the first half last night as the Raptors’ eyes got as wide seeing Jalen Brunson defend them as Auric Goldfinger’s were when he saw that shiny gold bar on the 18th green at Stoke Park. If there was a possession where Toronto didn’t attack Brunson in the first half, I seriously cannot remember it. The same goes for any offensive possession that didn’t end up with a late shot clock. It was really a desperate look at times, so desperate that Mike Brown even turned to a zone in the second half, called blitzes when Toronto barely crossed midcourt, and gave sparkplug Jose Alvarado the nod late in the third quarter. And as so often in the past, some of that stuff worked (we still do not like those traps, Mikey).With the game on the line, the Knicks turned into a rolling “Thunderball” that just couldn’t be stopped. Mikal Bridges locked down on defense for the second straight game, the backup point guard duelists provided numerous little plays, OG Anunoby smiled, and Landry Shamet once again looked like some cool device Q designed in an underground bunker – the red button unleashes movement threes and hellish defense on the opponent. And you have to deal with KAT and Brunson on top of all that? Good luck. When the orange and blue have it going like that, it seems as if they could even make some of those megalomaniac Bond villain plots for world supremacy work. Everything seems possible – even the Captain swatting shots and turning into Jalen Dikembe Mutombo Mpolondo Mukamba Jean-Jacques Wamutombo Brunson. RIP to the legend.Since “Diamonds Are Forever,” we really do not need a constant reminder of everything these Knicks are capable of; we still remember last year pretty well. That doesn’t mean it does not feel extremely awesome and puts a comfortable calm into a fan’s heart to see them clicking on all cylinders. It would be nice if these cylinders wouldn’t take three quarters to get going, but as long as the Knicks go home with goddess Victory, there’s nothing wrong with things the way they are. Just like there probably is nothing wrong with Robert Pattinson playing James Bond, so let us all wish him well.And let’s hope for him he’s not a Raptors fan.

item.title: 'Significant for cycling in the country' – British Cycling Ventures adds backing to City of London Nocturne in a bid to expand across Britain
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: British Cycling Ventures has announced a partnership with London City Nocturne organiser Koru Sports, with an eye on expanding the event to other British cities.Held over two days on the streets of the capital’s financial district, the City of London Nocturne comprises a series of criteriums, with the men’s and women’s elite races sanctioned by the UCI as Pro Criteriums. The 2027 event will be held on Friday 11 and Saturday 12 June next year, with the bulk of the racing happening on the second day. The partnership between organiser Koru Sports Group will aim to develop the event in the long term and accelerate the event’s commercial success, but it also provides the opportunity to expand the concept further afield."The venture will focus on expanding the reach of the Nocturne nationally," read a British Cycling press release. "Providing new opportunities to teams and riders, while complementing and elevating the existing domestic racing structure, including the Lloyds National Circuit Series. It will focus on enhancing fan experiences and reaching new audiences in key urban markets, while delivering a strong commercial programme for the Series."The City of London Nocturne first appeared on the capital’s streets in 2007 under the name of the Smithfield Nocturne, running as part of a wider festival of cycling for 11 years before returning in 2026 under the ownership of Koru Sports Group.The original event attracted riders such as Geraint Thomas, Mark Cavendish and Alex Dowsett, with Hannah and Alice Barnes both winning the women’s event, while the 2026 elite races were won by Matt Bostock (Rapha Cycling Club) and Nina Lavenu (AG Insurance-Soudal Devo). The event is not all about top-tier racing, however, with Pro-Am team races, folding bike, penny farthing and fixed-gear races, as well as those for lower categories of competitors.The original event was run by James Pope, who has a long history organising cycling events, including the long-running, but now defunct, Revolution track series, and now owns the Koru Sports Group, the organisation behind the revamped City of London Nocturne. "I’ve been privileged to have been organising cycling events for over two decades in the UK and have worked closely with British Cycling during this time," Pope said in a press release."The plans and ambition of British Cycling Ventures present an exciting opportunity to introduce a new major city racing concept in the UK starting with the City of London Nocturne. This partnership will help us create a new world-class city event format that will be a major boost to the UK racing scene, creating a fantastic experience for riders and cycling fans."British Cycling Ventures was launched in December 2025 as a commercial arm of the governing body, with the function of overseeing commercial growth, focusing on events across all disciplines."This is another significant moment in the major events vision of British Cycling Ventures, and the commercial growth of major city racing in the UK," said Managing Director Darren Henry."The innovation and plans for growth of the Nocturne from Koru Sports Group is significant for cycling in the country, and this joint venture brings together the best expertise in our sport to deliver huge impact through high-quality events. After hosting a brilliant event in the heart of London this year, it will continue to produce a spectacular atmosphere for riders and fans alike and make it an event not to be missed." item.title: One inspired transfer and one glaring miss – We analysed the data to see who won and lost in the women's 2025-2026 transfer market
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: With the women's peloton, the three-year promotion/relegation cycle that began this year is less important since fewer teams are competing for those WorldTour licences. However, transfers are still crucial to maintaining or improving the team's performance, getting high-profile results in races like the Tour de France Femmes and Paris-Roubaix Femmes and keeping or attracting sponsors.UAE Team l'IMAD ended the 2026 season as the world's number one team, just edging out FDJ United-Suez in the final days of the calendar with Maeva Squiban winning the Chrono des Nations and Elisa Longo Borghini landing on the podium at the Veneto Classic.Of course, FDJ United-Suez had a brilliant year with Demi Vollering taking out the Tour de France and World Championships, but also had plenty of success from riders like Juliette Berthet, Célia Gery, Elise Chabbey, Evita Muzic and Ally Wollaston.SD Worx-ProTime finished off the year as the third-best team, although it could have gone better had Lorena Wiebes not been disqualified from the Giro d'Italia due to her bike being underweight. The sprinter went on to win the green jersey in the Tour de France and two stages in addition to other WorldTour wins like In Flanders Fields and the Tour of Chongming Island.The Laboral Kutxa-Fundacion Euskadi squad quietly led the way among the ProTeams, ending the year in 13th in the UCI Team Rankings and finishing ahead of WorldTour teams Uno-X Mobility and Picnic-PostNL.The Spanish outfit saw Usoa Ostolaza land on the podium in the Vuelta a Burgos and take fourth overall in the Vuelta España, while other riders in the team picked up points in Continental and national championships and lower-level races throughout the year.However, the topic here is transfers, and FDJ United-Suez made the best hire of the 2025-2026 trades by bringing on German Franziska Koch, who went on to win Paris-Roubaix Femmes.The French team's recruitment strategy was hugely successful, giving the team a net gain of 3,753 points bringing in not only Koch but also Lauren Dickson as a neo-pro, Eva van Agt from Visma-Lease a Bike and, later in the season, mountain biker Kate Courtney.Leaving the team were Nina Buijsman, who went on to have a solid season with Human Powered Health, and Loes Adegeest, who had good results for Lidl-Trek.However, the addition of Koch was enormous. The German had a huge season after making the move from Picnic-PostNL, and even though she was often working to help Vollering win, Koch ended the season tenth in the UCI Individual Rankings.UAE Team l'IMAD also came out near the top in terms of transfer gains, with Mavi Garcia coming over from Liv-AlUla-Jayco and Megan Jastrab from Picnic-PostNL, more than offsetting the loss of Sofia Bertizzolo to FDJ. Visma-Lease a Bike also made strong gains, partially thanks to new signing Sarah Van Dam from the now-defunct Ceratizit team, ending the year fifth in the team rankings.At the other end of the spectrum, Picnic-PostNL were gutted in the transfer market. In addition to losing Charlotte Kool to Fenix-Premier Tech in a mid-season transfer last year, and Koch to FDJ, they saw Nienke Vinke leave for SD Worx-ProTime, and Jastrab head to UAE Team l'IMAD. They dropped to 17th in the UCI Team Rankings and suffered a net loss of 4,647 points. The Women's WorldTour is not as competitive during this cycle, with only 14 of the maximum 15 slots filled, and it's also uncertain if any of the ProTeams have the budget to apply for the WorldTour, so Picnic-PostNL may not be too concerned about their future. However, if Laboral Kutxa-Fundaction Euskadi - the top ProTeam in 13th this year - and Volkerwessels in 15th bid for WorldTour licenses, that could knock the German squad out of the WorldTour in 2029.Franziska Koch had a massive boost from her move in 2026, ending the season as the 10th best rider in the world. The German had clearly outgrown Picnic-PostNL, where she began making major strides in 2024 and 2025. Koch got a new coach after joining FDJ United-Suez, and said she thrived in the more relaxed, professional atmosphere when interviewed by Cyclingnews during the Spring Classics.Even while working as a valuable domestique for the world's top rider, Demi Vollering, Koch finished on the podium in Strade Bianche, and in the top 10 in the Tour of Flanders. Her main success of the year was a surprise victory in Paris-Roubaix over Marianne Vos and Pauline Ferrand-Prevot. She also became the double German champion and ended the year with the bronze medal in the time trial at Worlds. Koch earned 3,278.67 points this year, an improvement of 2,693 over last year, making her the most valuable transfer of 2026.Canadian Sarah van Dam was another rider who benefited greatly from a change of scenery. Her 2025 team Ceratizit went under, but Van Dam levelled up with Visma-Lease a Bike. Van Dam showed promise last year with a podium in the Itzulia Women, and continued her upward trajectory with Visma, taking fifth in the Tour Down Under, netting stage podiums in the Tour de Suisse and Vuelta España Femenina. She scored her first pro win in the late season at the Finistère Ladies Classic, and ended the season with podiums in the Giro dell'Emilia and Tre Valli Varesine.Lauren Dickson (FDJ United-Suez) was the third-highest scoring of the women transfers and the top neo-pro, winning the mountains classification at the Tour of Britain, a stage of the Faun Tour Femmes, and taking third in the Giro dell'Emilia along with strong stage results in Itzulia, the Giro d'Italia and Vuelta a Extremadura.The next-best neo-pro was Australian champion Mackenzie Coupland, who graduated from Liv's development team to the WorldTour Liv-AlUla-Jayco squad and scored top results in the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race, won the Vuelta a Extremadura, and finished fifth in the under-23 time trial at Worlds.Another notable new rider was Sandrine Tas, the former speed skater who signed with Lotto-Intermarché. She won two stages of the Bretagne Ladies Tour and finished second overall, then ended the year with a stage win in the Eneco Tour, too.The women's statistics tell an interesting story: Canyon-SRAM and Movistar scored all of their points with returning riders, which didn't happen in the men's teams. In the graph above their bubble size is miniscule, reflecting the fact that zero percent of the team's points came from incoming riders.As a percentage of their massive points, transfers didn't have as outsized of an impact on the top teams' rankings, but at the other end of the spectrum, incoming riders made a big difference for smaller teams.Lotto-Intermarché profited from the addition of speedskater Sandrine Tas, who quickly became a formidable sprinter with wins in the Bretagne Ladies Tour and Eneco Tour and a podium in the GP Stuttgart.Together, the team climbed nine places into 19th overall with 64.5% of their points coming from Tas and Linda Riedmann, winner of Binche-Chimay-Binche.St Michel-Preference Home-Auber93 made a bold move to sign former Paris-Roubaix winner Alison Jackson as part of a near-total revamp of their roster, with only four riders returning. They climbed up four places into 22nd.Transfers didn't work out quite as well for teams like Liv-AlUla-Jayco, who dropped three spots into 11th after losing Mavi Garcia to UAE, and Lidl-Trek, who dropped from fourth to sixth place after losing Lizzie Deignan and Ellen van Dijk to retirement and not finding riders of the same level to replace them.Because the women's teams can only score half of their maximum roster size, unlike the men's teams, where non-scored riders made next to no difference in their ranking of all riders' totals vs. the UCI Team Rankings, there were some significant differences for women.The total number of points scored by riders not making the top 10 of their team signals depth in the roster.UAE Team l'IMAD had the highest total points that didn't factor into their team rankings with 3,037. Of the transfers, Jastrab, with 646 and a top 10 in Paris-Roubaix, was among those not counting toward the team's total. Federica Venturelli (490 points) from the development squad was also a strong addition to UAE Team l'IMAD's depth.FDJ United-SUEZ seriously padded their roster, and in addition to Koch and Dickson's fine seasons, they brought on Evan van Agt and Kate Courtney, each of whom earned more than 300 points that weren't counted toward the team's rankings.Lidl-Trek, too, have great depth - their bottom ten riders scored 2,966 points - more than Picnic-PostNL's entire team! While most of that depth came from returning riders, incoming transfers Margot Vanpachtenbeke and Ricarda Bauernfeind scored over 300 points each that weren't part of the ranking total.AG Insurance-Soudal added to their depth, with a significant percentage of their total points not counting toward the UCI Team Rankings. While most of the uncounted points came from Gladys Verhulst, new hire Tess Moerman brought in 175 points that aren't reflected in their tally.There were very few transfer misses in the women's peloton, and the incoming riders who did not perform as they had in 2025 had very good reasons. Rooijakkers was down 623 points because she went on maternity leave after only a few racing days, while Dilyxine Miermont didn't perform for Picnic-PostNL after a strong year with Ceratizit in 2025 because of a bad crash in training.The main miss in the women's transfer market ahead of 2026 was Picnic-PostNL failing to retain their top talent or replace them with similar riders. They lost Koch, Vinke, and Jastrab, all riders who had brilliant 2026 seasons on other teams, which is quite concerning for the team's future. While returning riders Georgi and Nelson improved over 2025 and brought in 782 and 748 points, respectively, new hires Mia Griffin and Audrey De Keersmaeker scored only around 100 points. Six of their incoming riders scored fewer than 75 points, and most underperformed compared with last season.Another team that had a worrying transfer performance was EF Education-Oatly, who lost Alison Jackson and Letizia Borghesi. The Italian scored 920 points for AG Insurance-Soudal through top finishes in the Trofeo Alfredo Binda, Antwerp Port Epic and the Bretagne Ladies Tour, where she finished third overall. Jackson scored 422 points in a consistent but winless season for Auber 93.EF Education-Oatly's top transfer was Alice Towers with 244 points and a podium in Durango-Durango, but sprinter Alexis Magner was never able to reach her previous level after her horrific crash in 2025 and opted to retire at the end of the season.Next up, once the 2027 rosters are confirmed, we will see who stands to gain the most from the 2026-2027 transfer season for both men and women.One small note on the data: the UCI Team Rankings and the totals shown here may differ slightly because teams were given small penalties during the season. The difference was not enough to affect any of the conclusions.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Gent Six opening night drawn to a close early after heavy crash involving Jasper De Buyst
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: The opening night of the Gent Six track meet was stopped early on Tuesday after a major crash involving Jasper De Buyst and Jules Hesters during the final event.32-year-old De Buyst, in his final race before retiring, will now leave the sport earlier than planned after being taken to hospital following the crash. The Belgian underwent treatment on the track for several minutes before being taken away on a stretcher.De Buyst's Lotto-Intermarché team confirmed to that he has sustained a fractured collarbone in the fall and spent Tuesday night in the intensive care unit after a scan revealed internal bleeding around his spleen.Following the crash, which happened with three minutes and 50 laps remaining in the team pursuit event in the famous 't Kuipke velodrome, organisers consulted with the riders and decided not to restart.Lindsay De Vylder and Fabio Van Den Bossche hold the overall lead with 55 points, while Robbe Ghys and Yoeri Havik sit second on 41 points. Other notable competitors at the men's Gent Six include Tim Torn Teutenberg, Benjamin Thomas, and Bryan Coquard. Lotte Kopecky and Hélène Hesters headline the Ladies Cup on Friday.De Buyst called time on his 14-year road career this year, and will take on a new role at Lotto-Intermarché as performance manager. The Gent Six was set to be his farewell to racing."If I can finish with a good feeling, give my maximum, and above all have fun, then I will be a happy man on Sunday," he told earlier this week."The podium is the ambition again this year, although unlike in previous years, I am trying not to fixate on that. Of course, I dream of finishing the way it started: with a victory, but 13 years later. But then again, I can accept it if that doesn't happen."I have always had a special connection with Ghent. It is a kind of 'full circle' moment to say goodbye in Ghent. I will run into friends, family, former coaches, and current coaches during the week. It provides the opportunity to see everyone who helped build even the smallest part of your career."While De Buyst's time at the Gent Six and his racing career are now over, it doesn't mean that his partner Hesters also has to quit the race.Wednesday night's events are individual competitions, meaning Hesters can continue to compete while he looks for a new partner for the remaining days. Gent Six regulations stipulate that he'd have to leave the competition if he doesn't find a new partner within 48 hours.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down.
